items.title: Insignary Releases Free Insignary-Chk Tool to Detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell Exposure
items.author: CyberNewswire
items.content:
Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js

, a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js.

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely. Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases. Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images.

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution. The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued. insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the --fix option. It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify.

Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package. End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release. Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention.

The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image.

insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code. Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning. Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s --clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server.

“PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary. “We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.”

insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker. It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported.

Insignary Inc. is a Toronto-based cybersecurity company specializing in binary composition analysis and software supply chain security. Its patented technology enables organizations to identify open-source software components, vulnerabilities, and software provenance directly from compiled binaries without requiring access to source code. The company serves enterprises, governments, and software vendors worldwide and is backed by strategic investors and partners including BearingPoint in Europe, Cybertrust Japan and TechMatrix in Japan, and TMA Solutions. Through its global partner ecosystem, Insignary supports software supply chain security initiatives across North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information, visit .Contact

items.title: Before Moving Contracts Into Revenue Hub, Prove Who Will Send the Next Invoice.
items.author: Pratik Thakker
items.content:
Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Importing a contract and moving its billing are different operations. A team can reproduce an agreement's dates and line items accurately while leaving two systems prepared to charge for the same future period.

That is why a Revenue Hub migration should begin with the next invoice, not with the import file. The most consequential question is which system owns each future billing instruction, especially when the customer renews, expands, or changes terms during the transition.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would treat contract migration as a controlled transfer of responsibility. A successful import is one piece of evidence. The full acceptance test is whether the team can explain the active agreement, the next bill, the collection method, and the system responsible for each action without creating duplicates or losing history.

Separate visibility from billing ownership

HubSpot's direct-contract guide documents direct creation and import under a beta path. It distinguishes ordinary imports without billing schedules from a separate billing-continuity migration path. It also documents billing and collection configuration. Do not treat a record import as proof that recurring billing has moved.

The implementation model below is a proposal. Example registers, states, and test cases are not native HubSpot objects or a claim that every account can perform the same migration. Verify supported paths, eligibility, payment processing, and permissions in the account before planning a production cutover.

A visibility-only contract can be valuable. It can give customer-facing teams a view of the agreement while the established billing system remains authoritative. That is a legitimate architecture if the boundary is explicit and the record does not misleadingly suggest that HubSpot owns collection.

Build a responsibility register

For every agreement in scope, record the authoritative system for commercial terms, billing schedule, invoice issuance, collection, adjustments, and accounting export. Include a named owner and the evidence required to transfer each responsibility.

Do not use a single migration-complete flag for all six. A contract may be visible in HubSpot while collection remains external. An accounting connector may be reconciled while payment-method transfer is still unresolved. Those are separate states, not minor details beneath one green status.

An illustrative register might contain:

Terms and associations checked

Method and authorization verified

Correction trail retained

The chosen owner may remain the same for some rows. Migration does not have to mean moving every responsibility at once. It does require avoiding two active owners for one billable obligation.

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Capture the agreement as of a defined checkpoint. Include customer identity, billing entity, currency, term dates, recurring and one-time items, billing cadence, open invoices, approved adjustments, renewal terms, and pending amendments.

The baseline should distinguish committed terms from disputed or proposed changes. A salesperson's planned expansion is not an accepted amendment. A draft renewal is not the next active contract. An overdue invoice is not a reason to rewrite the commercial record to match the collected amount.

Reconcile the baseline with the people authorized to interpret it. Technical teams should not invent the treatment of unusual terms or decide how revenue should be recognized. Route accounting and legal questions to the appropriate owners, while documenting the resulting implementation decisions.

Freeze only the scope necessary for the cutover, and specify how urgent changes will be handled. An undocumented freeze creates shadow updates. A controlled exception process can preserve continuity without pretending the business will stop changing for the convenience of an import.

Classify amendments as dated revisions

An expansion, contraction, date correction, billing-contact update, and renewal are not interchangeable edits. Classify the change before choosing the mechanism that applies it.

HubSpot's contract overview describes change quotes and direct-edit paths with different requirements. It also states that an accepted renewal quote creates a new contract associated with the prior one. Those lifecycle relationships should be preserved rather than flattened into a single continually overwritten record.

For a hypothetical expansion, retain the agreement before the change, the approved amendment, the effective date, the affected line items, and the expected billing consequence. A proposed amendment can have a future effective date without changing what the customer owes for the current period.

Use separate evidence for agreement acceptance and system execution. The customer may approve a change before the billing system applies it. Conversely, a system edit may occur without sufficient business approval. Both mismatches should be visible in an exception queue.

Prove proration with fixtures, not intuition

Proration is a policy implemented through software. The result can depend on effective dates, billing periods, currencies, rounding, credits, and the treatment of previously issued invoices. A short arithmetic formula is not enough to describe every commercial arrangement.

HubSpot's contract setup documentation includes proration and renewal settings. Verify the actual configuration and supported behavior before modeling expected results. Do not assume an example from another account proves your account's outcome.

Build synthetic fixtures for a mid-period increase, a mid-period decrease, a future-dated change, a change near a renewal boundary, and a change after an invoice has already been issued. For each fixture, finance should approve the expected commercial treatment before the engineering test is judged.

Retain the calculation inputs and expected document sequence. When a result differs, classify whether the issue is a setting, an unsupported scenario, an incorrect expectation, or an implementation defect. Do not repair a test by manually changing the total until it looks plausible.

Keep invoice corrections and contract changes distinct

A billing correction does not necessarily amend the agreement. A contract amendment does not necessarily explain every historical invoice correction. Keeping both records prevents the team from erasing the distinction.

The contract management guide allows editing eligible manually associated invoices, but excludes subscription-created invoices and invoices automatically associated after quote acceptance. An eligible invoice amount edit does not update total contract value. That separation should inform reconciliation rather than be treated as a defect to eliminate through forced synchronization.

For example, imagine a hypothetical billing error that is corrected without changing the customer's agreed package. The correction trail should explain the invoice adjustment while leaving the approved commitment intact. If the customer also negotiated a package reduction, that is a second business event with its own effective date and approval.

Reporting should be able to represent both. If the system cannot explain why billed value differs from committed value, the team will eventually reconstruct the story from messages. That is a fragile substitute for a maintained evidence trail.

Design the cutover around a billing boundary

Choose a specific boundary for the transfer: which periods remain owned by the old system, which begin in the new system, and how straddling amendments will be handled. Document the treatment of open invoices separately from future billing.

The plan should identify each account's next expected invoice date, amount basis, responsible system, and collection path. Where exact amounts are not yet known, state why and identify the authoritative calculation source. Do not invent certainty for the sake of a migration checklist.

Before enabling new billing, verify that the old system will not independently issue the same obligation. Use supported controls and a reviewed procedure. Do not delete historical records to prevent future activity; history and scheduling are different concerns.

If the old system's state cannot be confirmed, stop the affected cohort. A delayed transfer with a named owner is safer than two teams each assuming the other has disabled billing. Preserve the obligation and its due date while resolving the uncertainty.

Avoid transferring payment responsibility by assumption

A payment method visible in one system is not proof that another system may use it. Availability, processor support, customer authorization, and migration constraints require separate verification through the approved payment-provider process.

Do not export or copy sensitive payment details into spreadsheets, prompts, or ordinary CRM fields. Keep payment operations within approved systems and involve the provider and finance owner for supported transfer paths.

Where the payment method cannot move through a supported process, the migration plan may require another collection arrangement. That is a customer-facing and financial decision, not a technical workaround an engineer should invent to complete the import.

Similarly, a sandbox demonstration cannot prove that production collection will behave correctly. Define what was tested, what remains unknown, and who must authorize any controlled production verification. No real charge should be initiated merely to make a technical checklist green.

A renewal should retain its relationship to the agreement it succeeds. Otherwise the business can count both as active commitments or lose the ability to explain the transition between them.

Create fixtures for a standard renewal, an early renewal with changed terms, a renewal while an amendment is pending, a canceled renewal, and an evergreen arrangement. Define which dates, values, and associations should be visible at each stage.

Do not assume that every agreement has a meaningful end date. A finite-term test suite is not enough to validate an evergreen population. Segment the migration by commercial shape and verify each supported path separately.

Also test the downstream account view. Customer success should be able to distinguish current entitlement from a proposed future package. Sales should see the renewal opportunity without interpreting it as already committed. Finance should retain the link between issued documents and the agreement revision that produced them.

Recover forward with evidence

A rollback plan should state what can be reversed and what cannot. A draft record may be editable. An invoice already delivered or a payment already collected may require a formal correction process rather than deletion.

Prepare an exception queue for duplicate schedules, missing associations, uncertain collection outcomes, mismatched terms, and unprocessed changes. Each exception needs an owner, a containment action, and a verification requirement.

If a timeout leaves the outcome of a consequential operation uncertain, inspect the owning system before repeating the operation. Retrying a read is different from retrying a create or charge. A migration tool should reflect that difference in its recovery procedure.

Keep a cutover journal with the cohort, checkpoint, decisions, verification evidence, and unresolved items. It need not be elaborate. It must remain usable when the engineer who performed the migration is unavailable and another person needs to explain the next bill.

Make the exit criteria about responsibility

The migration is ready when the team can answer five questions for every in-scope agreement: what is currently committed, which revision is active, who issues the next invoice, how collection is authorized, and where corrections are recorded.

Verify those answers after an amendment and a renewal, not only after the first import. Reconcile a sample forward from agreement to bill and backward from bill to approved terms.

Revenue Hub's newer contract capabilities expand the options for connecting commercial history with customer context. The implementation succeeds when those options produce one clear responsibility for the next obligation. A populated contract record is useful. A defensible billing handoff is the actual cutover.

Documentation checked October 20, 2026. This article proposes technical controls and does not provide accounting, legal, payment-provider, or tax advice. Verify beta eligibility and supported migration behavior in the relevant account.

items.title: Marvel's Wolverine Sells 2.4 Million Units: Is This Good or Bad?
items.author: Jose
items.content:
Just a few months ago, Marvel’s Wolverine was released to mixed reception. Some people thought the game was pretty good, while others thought that it was everything wrong with AAA gaming. But regardless of how they felt about it, a lot of people assumed that it didn’t matter if reception was mixed; the game was going to sell well anyways. Even I was on board this thought train. Well, as it turns out, that’s not really the case.

During Sony’s Q2 FY2026 Consolidated Financial Results speech, it was revealed that Marvel’s Wolverine sold 2.4 million units. Nowhere in the speech does it say that the company is disappointed with this number or that they were expecting it to be much higher. However, by just comparing it to the company’s previous titles, it’s obvious that this number is not in the same ballpark.

I compared it to previous Sony games. Take a look:

I couldn’t figure out how many units Marvel’s Spider-Man: Miles Morales sold within the first 50 days of its launch, or else I would’ve put it here. But let’s take a look at the other 3 games. Wolverine is trailing behind all three.

Although Ghost of Yotei is the highly anticipated sequel to a beloved game, I would’ve thought that Marvel and Wolverine’s brand recognition would’ve allowed it to surpass it. Then, we have to compare it to its predecessors, the Spider-Man games. I think most people would agree that Spider-Man is more well-known than Wolverine, but it’s not like he’s a C-list character or anything. It’s not surprising that Spidey’s games sold better, but it’s surprising that they sold way, way better.

By all counts, Marvel’s Wolverine should’ve been a smash hit. It was made by a studio that has developed a reputation as being video game adaptation studio. They had 3 great-selling games, with each game having a positive reception with fans and critics alike. Spider-Man 2 less so than the others, but at the time of its release, that game was being praised to the high heavens.

So, what happened? I think word of mouth killed the momentum of this game. Sure, the critics were mixed about it, but a lot of people choose to ignore reviews. However, what was really hurtful to the game’s reputation was what people were saying about it online. Those who’ve played it hated the story, repetitive gameplay, and the over-the-top hand-holding. Most importantly, I think a lot of people were just tired of PlayStation’s “cinematic game” formula. And unfortunately, for Marvel’s Wolverine, it was released at the wrong time.

Okay. We’ve looked at the game’s sales, compared it to similar titles, and talked about why it didn’t sell as much as it probably should’ve. We haven’t talked about the most important thing, though. Is 2.4 million units sold a good number for Marvel’s Wolverine?

The answer is: There’s no way this met sales expectations. When the studio’s previous games did way better in an even shorter timeframe, Wolverine’s sales can only be seen as disappointing. Nobody is saying that this game is a colossal flop and that Insomniac Games will shut down by the end of the year, but it’s safe to say that this game wasn’t the home run that Sony expected.

So, where do we go from here? Hopefully, Insomniac Games and PlayStation listen to the feedback and realize that the formula has to change. Fans have made it loud and clear that what worked 10 years ago won’t work now. I, for one, have faith that they can regroup and come back stronger for their next game.

items.title: Convenience Is the Price Tag on Your Privacy
items.author: Gaus Ahamad
items.content:
Friction used to protect us. We paid good money to get rid of it.

Nobody has ever woken up and decided to be tracked. Think about how strange that would be. No one opens an app store looking for the best way to let a company log which room they're in, who visits them, and what time they usually fall asleep.

What people look for is a faster way into an app. A doorbell that shows them the delivery guy. A phone that unlocks when they glance at it. A speaker that sets a timer while their hands are covered in flour.

Surveillance comes in the box. It isn't the product. It's the packing material, and nobody reads the packing material.

The usual way to tell this story is as a trade: you give up some data, you get a free service. That framing is too generous. A trade implies you knew the price and agreed to it. What actually happens is quieter. Every time a product removes a step from your life, it also removes a moment where you would have made a choice. And whoever removes the choice ends up making it for you.

That's the part worth sitting with. The thing we've spent twenty years eliminating, friction, was doing a job we never gave it credit for.

Friction was a privacy law nobody wrote down.

For most of history, privacy was protected by effort, not by rules. Tracking a person was expensive. Someone had to follow you, take notes, pull records from five different offices, and cross-reference them by hand. Your ordinary life stayed private because watching it was a pain.

Small daily inconveniences worked the same way. Typing a password meant you knew you were logging in. Paying cash meant the shopkeeper might know your face, but not your name, your bank, or the 400 other places you'd bought something. Walking to a friend's house left no record of the walk anywhere.

Each annoyance was a gate, and you noticed yourself passing through it.

Tech companies have spent two decades and a staggering amount of money tearing those gates down. Often, they were right to. Nobody misses the fax machine. But when you remove a step, you don't only remove the effort. You remove the noticing. And once you stop noticing, you stop deciding.

Designers have a name for interfaces built to trick you: dark patterns. Most of what this article describes isn't that. In a way it's harder to push back on, because it isn't a trick. It genuinely helps. That's exactly why nobody resists it.

The One-Tap Login: You didn't log in, you checked in.

"Continue with Google." "Sign in with Facebook." It saves you a password and maybe forty seconds.

To be fair, it's often more secure than the alternative. A big provider's login beats the same weak password reused across thirty sites. Security isn't the problem here. Linkage is.

Every time you use that button, the identity provider learns which apps and sites you use, and when. Your email account becomes a passport, and every app you open stamps it. The app on the other side gets something too: a verified, real identity, often with your name and photo, instead of a throwaway address it can't connect to anything.

Notice who benefits from those forty seconds. You get the time back once. The companies on both ends get a durable, linkable record for as long as they care to keep it.

There's also a power transfer that has nothing to do with data. If that one account gets suspended, by mistake or by an automated system that won't explain itself, you don't lose one service. You lose every door that key opened. People have been locked out of years of photos, work files, and dozens of linked logins over a flagged account they couldn't appeal to a human. Convenience put all your keys on one ring, then handed someone else the right to take the ring.

Apple's "Hide My Email" is a fair counterexample, a login shortcut built to leak less. But it proves the point. The default version of convenience leaks, and leaking less has to be designed on purpose.

The Smart Speaker: You bought a microphone and called it a timer.

Smart speakers are the cleanest example because the trade is so lopsided. The useful features are small: timers, weather, music, the odd trivia question. The cost is a networked microphone in the kitchen, the bedroom, the kid's room.

Companies say these devices only listen for the wake word, and that's mostly true. But "mostly" is carrying weight. Accidental activations happen. In 2019, it came out that Amazon, Google, and Apple all had human contractors reviewing samples of voice recordings, including clips people never meant to record. In 2023, Amazon agreed to pay $25 million to settle FTC charges that it kept children's Alexa recordings indefinitely and used them to improve its algorithms.

Of course they hadn't. It was buried deep in a menu. That's the friction argument running in reverse: when privacy is the option that takes effort, almost nobody picks it, and then the low number becomes the excuse to remove it.

The bigger lesson is what buying the device actually means. You don't make one decision. You make a decision once, and the company keeps making decisions about that device for years. The terms update. A setting disappears. A feature you never asked for arrives overnight. The hardware sits in your house, but its rules live on someone else's server.

That is the real price of convenience. Not the data on the day you plug it in. The permanent right of someone else to change the deal.

The Doorbell: Your porch joined someone else's network.

Video doorbells sold peace of mind. See who's there. Catch the package thief.

But a camera pointed at your porch also points at the street, the sidewalk, your neighbor's driveway, and everyone who walks past. You agreed to that. They didn't.

Amazon's Ring spent years building ties with police. By mid-2022, 2,161 law enforcement agencies could ask Ring owners for footage through its Neighbors platform. That same year, in a letter to Senator Ed Markey, Amazon admitted it had handed footage to police without the owner's consent or a warrant 11 times, citing emergency exceptions. In 2023, the FTC separately alleged that Ring employees and contractors had been able to access customers' private videos.

Ring's police policies have been reworked more than once since then. The specifics keep shifting. The structure doesn't: once your footage lives on a company's server, what happens to it depends on that company's policies, its lawyers, and whatever pressure it's under that quarter.

Nobody installing a doorbell thinks they're joining a neighborhood surveillance grid. But millions of separate purchases built one anyway. No vote, no public debate. Just a lot of people who wanted to see the delivery guy.

Face Unlock: The honest exception that proves the rule.

It would be lazy to claim every convenience is a privacy disaster. Some aren't.

Face ID on an iPhone keeps your face data in a secure chip on the phone itself. It isn't uploaded to Apple's servers. Most phone fingerprint readers work the same way. In that design, you get the convenience, and the company never gets your face.

So why bring face unlock up at all? Because it trained hundreds of millions of people to feel relaxed about something that used to feel invasive: a machine scanning your face to decide whether you get in.

That comfort doesn't stay on the phone. It travels to airport gates, stadium entrances, office turnstiles, and shops, where your face is rarely stored on a chip you own. Clearview AI built a face search engine from billions of photos scraped off the open web and sold access to police. Not one person in that database ever pressed "unlock."

The lesson isn't "face unlock is bad." It's that the same convenience can be built to keep power with you or to move it away, and from the outside you usually can't tell which. Both feel identical. You look at a screen, and it works.

The pattern underneath all of it.

Line the examples up and the same shape shows up every time.

  1. The benefit is immediate, small, and yours. Forty seconds saved. A timer set. A package spotted.
  2. The cost is delayed, cumulative, and spread thin. A profile that grows. A dataset that gets sold, breached, or subpoenaed. A policy that changes in year three.
  3. The control sits with whoever runs the server. Not with whoever owns the device.

That third point matters most. We talk about privacy as if it's about secrets, as if the question is "do I have something to hide?" It's really about leverage. Whoever holds the record of your habits can predict you, price you, nudge you, and in the worst case, lock you out.

Every convenience that runs through someone else's system adds a little to their leverage and takes a little from yours. No single tap matters. That's exactly why it works. Power rarely moves in one big grab anymore. It moves in a billion small, reasonable, time-saving decisions.

One more mechanism makes all this hard to undo: convenience only turns one way.

Once you've used one-tap checkout, typing a card number feels absurd. Once the lights respond to your voice, getting up to flip a switch feels primitive. Each convenience resets your baseline, and the old way starts to feel like a punishment.

Companies understand this well. The first version of a feature is often generous, private, cheap, or free. By the time the terms tighten, the price rises, or the data practices change, you're no longer comparing the product to nothing. You're comparing it to going back. Almost nobody goes back.

That's how a choice becomes a dependency. Not by force. By habit.

So what do you actually do?

Nobody is going to throw their phone in a lake, so that advice is useless. The goal isn't zero convenience. It's choosing your conveniences on purpose instead of accepting them by default.

• Ask where it runs. On-device features (local face unlock, offline voice processing, end-to-end encrypted backups) keep power with you. Cloud-dependent ones hand it to someone else. When a local option exists, the small extra effort is usually worth it.

• Don't put every key on one ring. A password manager is nearly as fast as "Continue with Google," and one suspended account can't take your whole digital life down with it.

• Make microphones and cameras earn their spot. A smart speaker in the kitchen might be worth it to you. In the bedroom or the kids' room, probably not.

• Keep a little friction you can live with. Skip "remember this device" on accounts that matter. Turn off auto-sync for things that don't need it. Take the login that costs ten extra seconds. Small annoyances bring back small moments of choice.

• Re-check after updates. The deal you agreed to is not the deal you have now. A five-minute settings review twice a year catches most of the quiet changes.

• Pay when you can. Paying doesn't guarantee privacy. But a product that earns money from you directly has less reason to earn it from you indirectly.

None of this makes you invisible. It just means you're spending your privacy instead of having it spent for you.

Convenience isn't evil. It's one of the best things technology does. Hours that used to disappear into queues, paper forms, and hunting for keys now go somewhere better. That's real.

But nothing engineered this well is free. The cost just isn't printed on the receipt. It shows up in who gets to make decisions about your life after you've stopped paying attention.

Every shortcut is a small handoff. Make enough of them without looking, and one day you'll notice that a lot of choices about your home, your face, your voice, and your movements are being made by people you've never met, on servers you'll never see, under terms that change whenever they like.

You didn't choose surveillance. You chose the shortcut. Just remember that every shortcut leads somewhere, and it's worth knowing whose road you're on.

1) Is every convenient feature bad for privacy?

No. Features that process data on your device, like Face ID or local fingerprint unlock, give you the convenience without sending your data to a company. The risk grows when a feature depends on someone else's servers.

2) Is "Sign in with Google" unsafe?

Not in the security sense. It's often safer than reusing weak passwords. The trade-off is that it links your activity across apps to one account, and losing that account can lock you out of everything tied to it.

3) Do smart speakers record everything I say?

They listen locally for a wake word, then send what follows to the cloud. Accidental activations do happen, and since March 2025 some Echo models no longer offer an option to keep processing on the device.

4) What's the easiest privacy upgrade that doesn't kill convenience?

A password manager instead of social logins, plus a quick review of which rooms have cameras and microphones. Both take under an hour and cost almost no daily convenience.

items.title: “We Love Our Tops and Bottoms”: The 25 Wildest Quotes From Grindr CEO George Arison’s AMA
items.author: Clapback
items.content:
George Arison took Grindr’s earnings story to r/wallstreetbets. Reddit responded with memes, pointed questions, and the occasional surprisingly candid answer.

On November 6, [Grindr CEO George Arison hosted an ask-me-anything session](https://www.reddit.com/r/wallstreetbets/comments/1xpgjl2/im_george_arison_ceo_of_grindr_grnd_we_reported/ .) in r/wallstreetbets after the company reported third-quarter results. He came to discuss the publicly traded company’s future as a consumer AI platform, its nearly 16 million monthly users, and its expansion into healthcare. The subreddit had other ideas.

The thread mixed earnest questions about privacy and ads with relentless innuendo about stock-market “bears,” fast-food dumpsters, and the company’s name. Below are 25 of the most memorable exchanges and comments, with Arison’s responses identified separately from Reddit jokes and unverified allegations.

The bluntest question was also among the thread’s most popular. It set the tone for a Q&A where no corporate talking point was safe. It was the most direct possible collision between a corporate earnings tour and Reddit culture. The question became a referendum on whether a CEO could survive a forum that treats every setup as an invitation to meme. Arison did not answer this particular one in the supplied transcript.

2. “This is where the magic happens.”

Asked why he chose wallstreetbets rather than a more conventional community, Arison supplied the most concise possible defense of the venue. That four-word reply is arguably the clearest evidence that Arison understood the assignment. WallStreetBets is not an obvious investor-relations venue for a dating platform; it is a place where a ticker symbol and a punchline can become the same thing. Rather than apologize for the choice, he embraced the chaos.

3. “Grindr does not crash ;)”

A user asked about supposed outages during Republican National Conventions. Arison’s playful denial did not establish anything about traffic at political events. The joke leaned on recurring internet rumors about spikes in Grindr use during Republican political gatherings. His wink turned a loaded question into a brand moment, but it should not be mistaken for independent evidence about usage at conventions. The distinction matters: the question was a joke, the answer was a denial.

4. “We love our tops and bottoms”

A question about top-line versus bottom-line growth earned a reply that was both on-brand and almost completely devoid of financial guidance. This was a genuine question about financial performance disguised as a perfect double entendre. Arison answered with a line engineered for screenshots. For investors looking for margin guidance, it offered precisely zero basis points of insight; for everyone else, it was the AMA’s most shareable earnings commentary.

5. “I’ve actually never eaten at Wendy’s”

A wallstreetbets question invoked the subreddit’s favorite fast-food chain and its dumpster lore. Arison took the bait, then pivoted to inflation. Wendy’s is a recurring landmark in WallStreetBets humor, where failed trades are imagined ending behind the restaurant’s dumpster. Arison’s confession that he had never eaten there briefly made the CEO sound like a tourist visiting Reddit’s national monument. Then he did something stranger: he answered the economics part seriously.

6. “But no, $20 is not $20.”

Arison turned a crude running joke into a surprisingly serious comment about affordability and housing access. In the same reply, Arison moved from a $20 joke to housing affordability. It was a whiplash-inducing pivot from meme economics to actual economics, and one of the rare moments when the CEO sounded less like a corporate spokesperson than a person with a view on public policy.

7. “I paid for premium membership for 2 years without realizing it. I’m not even gay”

The commenter asked for a refund. No CEO answer appears in the supplied thread excerpt. The commenter claimed to have paid for a subscription for two years without using the service, then asked whether a refund was still possible. It is an absurd customer-support ticket to bring to an earnings AMA, but it also highlights the awkwardness of subscription businesses: revenue can keep arriving long after a customer stops paying attention. No refund decision was shown.

8. “Grindr has an exposed backend”

The pun appeared beneath a commenter’s allegation about a past security interview and subsequent breach. The underlying allegation is not verified by the AMA transcript. The pun followed a far more serious, unverified allegation about a security interview and a subsequent data incident. Reddit immediately converted the phrase “exposed backend” into innuendo. That tonal switch captures the entire thread: potentially consequential privacy questions competing with the urge to make the next joke.

Behind the jokes was a consequential challenge about protecting sensitive user data. The supplied excerpt does not show Arison answering this specific question. This was one of the AMA’s strongest questions because Grindr handles information that can be unusually sensitive. The commenter described a personal interview experience and alleged a later breach; those claims should not be treated as established facts without separate reporting. The question itself remains important, and the provided excerpt contains no direct answer to it.

10. “We maintain an internal ‘dangerous neighborhoods’ list”

In a separate security answer, Arison described safeguards in higher-risk countries, including hiding distance, blocking screenshots of certain media, and removing third-party ads. Arison’s detailed response to another user gave a rare look at how the company says it adapts product features to legal and physical risks. Turning off distance and discovery features, restricting screenshots, and removing third-party advertising are concrete design choices, not just a promise to take privacy seriously. The safeguards are the company’s description and deserve independent scrutiny.

11. “Gay people are like everyone else.”

Asked whether gay people like AI, Arison pushed back on the premise before suggesting gay men often adopt new technology early. Asked whether gay people like AI, Arison rejected the idea that a diverse community shares one view. He then offered a more provocative business thesis: gay men have historically been early technology adopters. His iPhone anecdote was presented as an analysis he had encountered, not as a verified figure in the AMA.

12. “People produce about 50+ messages a day on average”

The CEO’s engagement claim helped explain why he describes Grindr as an open social network rather than a swipe-to-match dating app. The claim is one of the most consequential numbers in the discussion. If an average user sends more than 50 messages daily, Grindr is selling investors engagement and network effects, not simply swipes or dates. It also helps explain why the company wants to add services around existing conversations rather than build a separate audience from scratch.

13. “We are more of a social network for gay people vs. a dating product”

This distinction was the backbone of his business pitch: expand from dating into travel, community, AI services, and healthcare. This is the strategic repositioning behind the jokes. Dating apps are often judged on matching and churn; social networks are judged on ongoing utility, identity, and community. Arison wants Grindr in the second category, which would justify building adjacent products even after a user finds a partner.

14. “Grindr ‘was about sex.’”

Arison said a large financial firm had declined to work with Grindr for that reason, and called the attitude fundamentally homophobic. This is his account of the exchange. Arison said a large financial firm once declined to work with Grindr because it was “about sex,” a rationale he characterized as homophobic. The story reframes a commercial objection as a question of whether gay-focused products are treated differently from mainstream dating businesses. The firm was not named in the AMA.

15. “We are responsible for a quarter of gay relationships in the United States.”

A striking company claim emerged in an answer about why successful relationships need not hurt retention. A quarter of gay relationships is an enormous claim about cultural reach, and it came in response to a question about whether successful relationships hurt retention. Arison’s argument was that couples can still use Grindr for friends, travel, and community. The percentage is his claim; the transcript does not provide the underlying study.

The strongest conventional management advice in the thread: choose two to four priorities instead of trying to do everything. This is probably the most reusable management advice in the entire exchange. His point was not that ideas are scarce, but that attention is. The CEO said he tries to identify two to four priorities at a time and refuse distractions, a surprisingly disciplined philosophy in an AMA overflowing with them.

17. “I’ve become much more of a Reddit user recently because so much of the content you get from AI is from Reddit”

An unexpected explanation of why the CEO has been spending more time on the platform. There is a wonderfully recursive quality to this answer: an AI-focused CEO goes to Reddit partly because AI draws from Reddit. It also hints at a distribution shift. Forums are not just communities to speak to; they are increasingly part of the text ecosystem that shapes how people encounter information through AI products.

18. “This has been far more serious than I expected!”

Despite the chaos, Arison said the AMA contained more substantive discussion than he anticipated. It is hard to imagine what a CEO expects from WallStreetBets when introducing a publicly traded app whose name practically writes its own jokes. Yet Arison said the discussion was more serious than anticipated. That may be the strongest compliment the forum received all afternoon.

19. “One of the things that makes that possible is ads”

Responding to complaints about intrusive ads, Arison argued advertising helps keep Grindr free for 93% of users, while acknowledging the ad experience needs work. The advertising exchange exposed a real tension in the business. Arison defended ads as the mechanism that keeps the product free for most users while acknowledging the challenge of attracting direct advertisers. Users complaining about intrusive ads and a CEO defending free access can both be describing the same trade-off.

20. “My husband is an public health doctor who spent decades working on HIV”

Arison connected Grindr’s health ambitions to his family and to the company’s acquisition of telehealth provider Freddie. The Freddie acquisition was more than a growth talking point for Arison. He connected Grindr’s HIV-prevention ambitions to his husband’s long career in public health. That personal link gives the healthcare expansion an unusually human motivation, even as it remains a commercial initiative requiring execution.

21. “The Global Gayborhood”

The company’s aspirational phrase for a platform that encompasses more than dating, including an AI-powered premium tier and healthcare. “Global Gayborhood” sounds like branding, but it is also an acquisition strategy in two words. Grindr wants to be the starting point for multiple services serving gay men, with AI premium features and HIV-prevention healthcare as early examples. The challenge is expanding without eroding trust in the core app.

22. “I knew I was gay pretty early”

In one of the more personal answers, Arison described growing up in Soviet Georgia, coming out, and building a family with his husband. The most personal answer of the AMA traced Arison’s childhood in Soviet Georgia, where he said being openly gay did not feel possible, to his life as a husband and father. In a thread full of jokes about whether he uses the product, it was a reminder that his relationship with the company’s mission is not merely financial.

23. “Do you have a team reviewing each of your responses, or are you just raw dogging this”

Perhaps the perfect summary of the tension between a polished public-company AMA and the language of wallstreetbets. A surprisingly fair question, buried inside a phrase no corporate communications team would put in a briefing document. The AMA excerpt does not show an answer, so readers are left to judge the tone of the responses for themselves. The very fact that a CEO entertained this forum made the question inevitable.

Grindr trades under GRND. Showing up on the subreddit best known for retail-trading frenzies made the question inevitable. For a community obsessed with stocks becoming memes, the possibility that Grindr had deliberately wandered into meme-stock territory was too good to ignore. The question captures the risk of this kind of investor outreach: attention is easy to generate, but impossible to control once the comments take over.

25. “Can it flirt in rust?”

The user asked whether Grindr Edge was Claude-powered, then delivered a programming-language punchline. The excerpt includes no answer. The final joke combines the company’s AI push with a programming-language punchline. It is also a neat summary of the gap between a product roadmap and internet reception. The joke density was enormous, but the serious topics were substantial: how Grindr handles sensitive data, whether advertising has damaged the free experience, what AI will actually do for users, and whether healthcare can become a meaningful second business. items.title: Load Balancing Starts Before the Load Balancer: Routing Patterns for Distributed Systems
items.author: Varsha Ganesh
items.content:
This is the third in my series on control plane architecture and design patterns. See the first article on a high-level overview of control planes , and the second on the scaling component .

I ended my last piece on scaling with a promise to come back to hot partitions, i.e., the situation where a single piece of your system is hit with disproportionate traffic no matter how well the rest of your infrastructure is provisioned. That problem lives squarely in load balancing and routing, which is what I want to dig into here.

The thing that surprised me most when I actually started building these systems is how little "load balancing" has to do with load balancers, once you get past the simplest cases. A load balancer is one tool for solving a routing problem. It's not the only one, and for a lot of distributed systems, it's not even the primary one.

The Simple Case: Fronting Stateless Services

For a basic web application, load balancing is close to what most people picture:

  • DNS-based load balancing -  multiple A records pointing to different IPs, with clients or resolvers distributing requests across them. It's cheap and simple, but coarse: you get little control over how traffic is actually distributed, and DNS on its own has no real-time awareness of backend health. Many DNS providers let you associate health checks with your records so that unhealthy IPs get pulled out of rotation, which closes part of that gap. But those checks aren't free: each one is a probe you pay for and have to tune, and the cost grows with the number of endpoints and the frequency you check them. They also have no global view of the system. A check can tell you whether an endpoint responds, but not how loaded it is, how it compares to its peers, or whether pulling it out of rotation will overload the ones that remain.
  • A dedicated load balancer or proxy (an ALB, an NLB, nginx, Envoy) sitting in front of your fleet, actively health-checking backends and routing each connection or request according to an algorithm, e.g., round robin, least connections, weighted, or latency-based.

For stateless, interchangeable backends, this gets you most of the way there. Any healthy instance can serve any request, so the algorithm mostly just needs to avoid overloading any single one.

This is also where most teams' mental model of "load balancing" stops. It's worth pushing past that, because the moment your backend isn't stateless and interchangeable, this model stops being sufficient.

The Harder Case: Routing With State

A distributed database doesn't have interchangeable backends. Each host owns specific partitions of data, and a request for a given key has to go to the host that actually holds it (or a replica of it). You can't round-robin your way out of that.  The routing decision is now coupled to , which is a placement problem, not a traffic-distribution problem.

This is where load balancing stops being about the request path and starts being about the partitioning and placement strategy decided when data is written, long before any request shows up.

Placement Strategy Is Load Balancing in Advance

When a new table or dataset is created in a system like Cassandra, the control plane decides how its partitions get distributed and replicated across the fleet. Get that placement strategy wrong, and no amount of clever request routing fixes it later. You've already baked an imbalance into where the data lives.

Good placement strategies generally try to:

  • Spread partitions evenly across available hosts, so no single host owns a disproportionate share of the dataset
  • Respect replication and fault-domain constraints simultaneously - replicas of the same partition shouldn't land on the same rack or availability zone, even while you're optimizing for even distribution
  • Account for heterogeneous hardware; if your fleet isn't uniform, a host with double the capacity should reasonably get more partitions than one with less

None of this touches the request path directly. It's load balancing that happens at write time, and it's arguably the more important half of the problem.

The Problem Placement Alone Can't Solve: Hot Partitions

Even a well-designed placement strategy runs into a specific failure mode: hot partitions. This happens when traffic to specific keys is wildly uneven, usually because of a poorly chosen partition key (a timestamp, a low-cardinality value, a celebrity user ID) that concentrates requests onto one partition regardless of how evenly the was distributed.

The uncomfortable part is that this isn't something you can fully prevent through upfront design. Traffic patterns shift, applications evolve, and a key that was fine at launch can become a hotspot a year later. Detecting and correcting for it has to be an ongoing, automated function of the control plane, not a one-time decision.

  • Per-partition metrics, not just aggregate fleet metrics such as throughput, request count, and latency broken down at the partition level, since fleet-wide averages will hide a hot partition sitting next to a dozen idle ones
  • A threshold model that distinguishes a genuinely overloaded partition from normal variance. Naive fixed thresholds tend to either fire constantly on noisy workloads or miss slow-building hotspots
  • Attribution, ideally, knowing keys within a partition are driving the load helps decide whether splitting the partition will actually help, or whether the hot key will just follow you into the new split

Correcting for It: Re-Partitioning Live

Once a hot partition is identified, the fix is usually to split it and redistribute the pieces, but doing this against a partition serving live production traffic is one of the more delicate operations a control plane performs. A few things matter here:

  • The split has to be incremental and reversible. Splitting a partition in one atomic step against live traffic is asking for an outage; the operation needs to be able to pause, resume, or roll back mid-flight.
  • Routing has to update consistently with the split, so requests during the transition land on the correct new partition rather than the stale one. This usually means a routing/metadata layer that's updated as part of the same operation, not after it.
  • The new partitions need to actually solve the problem. If the hot key itself is the issue rather than uneven key distribution, splitting the partition just relocates the hotspot rather than resolving it. Sometimes the real fix is upstream, in how the application chooses partition keys in the first place.

Systems like DynamoDB build this kind of adaptive re-partitioning directly into their control plane, specifically so that a single misbehaving key doesn't require manual intervention every time it happens.

The Pattern Shows Up Everywhere Stateful Systems Do

Databases are the clearest illustration of placement-time routing, but the same problem, and largely the same solutions, show up anywhere a system shards state across a fleet. Two examples worth knowing well, because they each stress the pattern in a different direction.

A distributed cache like Redis Cluster or Memcached with consistent hashing looks superficially like the database case: keys are hashed to determine which shard owns them, and requests get routed accordingly. But caches diverge from databases in one important way that reshapes the whole routing problem - cache misses are cheap enough to tolerate, but hot keys are far more common and far more punishing.

Because caches sit in front of a slower system of record, a single viral key (a trending post, a flash-sale product, a piece of session data for a suddenly-popular event) can spike orders of magnitude above normal traffic in seconds, not the gradual drift you'd see with a hot database partition. A few things follow from that:

  • Consistent hashing helps with rebalancing, not hot keys. It minimizes how many keys move when you add or remove a shard, but it does nothing to stop one key from being disproportionately hot. The hash function doesn't know or care about request volume.
  • Client-side or edge-level request coalescing often matters more here than server-side re-sharding. If ten thousand requests for the same key arrive in the same second, the fix usually isn't "move this key to its own shard" (by the time you've detected and acted on it, the spike may already be over),  it's collapsing concurrent requests for the same key into one upstream fetch.
  • Local caching layers in front of the shard tier (an in-process cache on each application host, for instance) can absorb a hot-key spike before it ever reaches the sharded layer at all, which is often a simpler fix than trying to make the sharded routing layer reactive enough to keep up.

The routing decision for a cache miss is still a placement problem, i.e., determination of which shard owns this key. The operational fix for a hot key, however, usually lives one layer up from the routing logic itself, in how aggressively you can avoid sending duplicate requests downstream in the first place.

Systems like Kafka consumer groups or Flink jobs route by partition, much like a sharded database. A message with a given key is deterministically assigned to a partition, and a specific consumer or task instance owns that partition for processing.

But the load balancing constraint here is different in a way that matters: ordering guarantees typically require that all messages for a given key are processed by the same partition, in order, which means you can't rebalance a hot partition by simply splitting it the way you might with a database.

This creates a distinct set of routing trade-offs:

  • Partition count is usually a fixed, upfront decision. Unlike a database that can dynamically split an overloaded partition, most stream processing systems set partition count at topic-creation time, because increasing it later changes the key-to-partition mapping and can break ordering guarantees for existing consumers mid-stream. Getting this number right up front matters more here than almost anywhere else in the stack. Under-provision partitions and you have a hot-partition problem you architecturally cannot fix without a disruptive migration. Over-provisioning is the safer mistake, but it isn't free either: every partition carries its own log segments, file handles, and replication state on the brokers, so a very high count slows recovery after a broker failure (more partitions need new leaders), makes consumer group rebalances more disruptive, and shrinks producer batches, which hurts efficiency and latency. It also won't rescue you from a single hot key, since a given key always maps to one partition no matter how many exist. The practical target is enough headroom for foreseeable growth in consumer parallelism, not an arbitrarily large number "to be safe."
  • Consumer-side scaling is bounded by partition count, not by consumer group size. Adding more consumers than partitions doesn't help. The extra consumers just sit idle, so "scaling" a stream processing system often means capacity planning for partition count well ahead of actual load, rather than reactively adding resources the way you would with a stateless service.
  • Skewed key distribution is a design-time problem, not a runtime one. Because you can't cheaply reshuffle partitions after the fact, uneven key distribution (one customer ID generating 100x the events of any other) has to be addressed either in how keys are chosen, or by explicitly over-partitioning for the skew you expect by anticipating the hot path rather than reacting to it.

Stream processors push placement-time routing to its logical extreme: nearly all of the load balancing work happens at design time, because the ordering guarantees that make the system useful are exactly what make runtime rebalancing so constrained.

Load balancing in a distributed system operates on two timelines that are easy to conflate:

  • Request-time routing - the classic load balancer problem, distributing incoming requests across available, healthy backends
  • Placement-time routing - deciding, before any request arrives, where data or resources live in the first place, and continuously correcting that placement as traffic patterns change

For stateless services, the first one is basically the whole problem. For anything stateful and partitioned, the second one dominates, and it's a control plane responsibility that runs continuously in the background rather than a configuration you set once and forget.

Next in this series, I'll get into reliability guarantees - how control planes enforce promises (replication, TTL-based deletion, eventual consistency) that are genuinely hard to guarantee synchronously in the request path, and the auditing systems teams build to catch the gap between what a system promises and what it actually did.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon Is Locked: Here's What It Means for Your Budget and Your Patch Window
items.author: Ifeoluwa Tech (PhD)
items.content:
If you build software for a living, you probably cannot use it yet. Carbon is going first to a small group of cyber defenders through Google's Fairwind Program while it goes through US government pre-release testing. Developers and businesses get it later, and Google has not said when.

I went through the independent test data, the security research behind Carbon's benchmarks, and Google's own launch notes. Two things matter far more for most of us than who sits at number one. The first is what this class of model will cost to run. The second is what it means for how quickly we need to patch our own code.

What Carbon Costs Per Task

Leaderboards tell you which model scored highest. They rarely tell you what it costs to get that score, and for a startup running agents all day, that is the number that decides whether a model is usable.

Artificial Analysis publishes exactly that. Running its full Intelligence Index, Carbon cost. Claude Opus 5.5 at its highest setting cost $10.04, and GPT-6 Astra at its highest setting cost $6.25.

Scale that to a team running 10,000 hard agent tasks a month and the gap becomes real money:

Model (highest reasoning setting)

A word of caution before anyone builds a budget on this. These are costs on a demanding evaluation suite at standard prices, so your own workload will differ. Treat them as a comparison between models, not a quote. Google is also offering Carbon at half price at launch, $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, before it rises to $4 and $20.

The more interesting detail is why Carbon is cheaper than Opus. It used about 123,000 output tokens per task against 173,000 for Opus 5.5. A model that reaches the answer with fewer tokens saves money on every single call, and for agent loops that run for hours, that adds up faster than any headline discount.

Where It Wins and Where It Doesn't

Carbon is not the best at everything, and the independent data shows where.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, it scored 59, second behind Claude Code running Opus 5.5 at 62. It also came second on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 64%, and on FrontierCode with 51% against 56% for Opus. If your product is mainly an autonomous coding agent, Carbon is a strong option, not an automatic upgrade.

Reliability is the other number to watch. Carbon is more accurate than Google's previous model on the Artificial Analysis knowledge benchmark, but its hallucination rate rose from 4% to 11%. That is still the second lowest of any model tested, behind only Argon. In practice, it means Carbon knows more but guesses more when it does not know. If your app depends on factual answers, keep a verification step in place.

Why It's Gated: Attackers Are Getting Faster

The reason most of us are waiting is in Carbon's cybersecurity scores. Google says it found real vulnerabilities in 88.2% of SEC-bench Pro cases, patched them at the root cause in 71.0% of CWE-bench cases, and turned flaws into working exploits in 54.8% of ExploitGym cases. Those tests were run "without guardrails."

That last benchmark is the uncomfortable one. A model that can turn a bug into an attack is useful to defenders testing their own systems, and just as useful to the people they are defending against.

This did not appear overnight. In 2024, Daniel Kang's group at the University of Illinois showed that GPT-4 could exploit 87% of a set of 15 known vulnerabilities when given the public description, and just 7% without it. Every other model they tested scored zero.

By May 2026, a 16-author team including Dawn Song and Nicholas Carlini had built ExploitGym from 898 real vulnerabilities across userspace programs, Google's V8 engine and the Linux kernel. They found that exploitation is still hard, but frontier agents now succeed on a meaningful share of cases, even with common defences turned on.

Meanwhile, human attackers were already speeding up. Google's Mandiant team exploited in 2023 and found the average time from disclosure to exploitation had fallen to about five days. In 2018 and 2019, it was 63. Seventy per cent were exploited as zero-days, before a patch existed.

Put those two trends together, and the logic behind gating Carbon is easy to follow. Google wants the patching capability in defenders' hands before anything similar becomes widely available. Anthropic made the same call in April when it limited Claude Mythos Preview to its Project Glasswing partners, and has since widened access to about 150 more organisations in more than 15 countries. Neither model is public.

What You Can Do Before It Opens

Here is the part I think matters most. Most teams reading this will not be on a Fairwind or Glasswing list, and attackers will not wait for the general release. So what can a small engineering team actually do this month?

Use what is already available. Gemini 4 Argon has been on the paid Gemini API since 13 October. Google's agent, which upstreamed 72 security fixes to open-source projects as large as 4.5 million lines in its first six months, can be run with public models by any Google Cloud customer, according to Google's.

Patch what is known to be exploited first. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue held as of August 2026. If a dependency you ship is on it, that comes before any new feature.

Prioritise by difficulty, not headlines. Mandiant found no reliable link between media coverage and how fast a bug is exploited. What mattered was how easy the exploit was and how valuable the target. An easy bug in a payment flow deserves more urgency than a famous one that is hard to use.

Assume the window is days, not weeks. Automated dependency updates, fuzzing in your build pipeline and network segmentation all buy time when a patch is not ready.

Ask to get in. Fairwind says it is staged for governments, critical infrastructure and core technology platforms, with more than 650 partners so far. If your company runs infrastructure other people depend on, it is worth asking.

Gating Carbon is the right decision. A strong exploit writer released to everyone on day one would hand attackers a head start that defenders could not close.

But it leaves an open question for the rest of us. Fairwind's published priorities name large institutions. Glasswing's expanded list reached Europe, North America and parts of Asia. Smaller companies, independent researchers and teams in places like Lagos or Nairobi are not clearly covered by either. If the best defensive tools reach well-funded organisations first, the gap between the well-defended and everyone else could widen just as attacks get cheaper.

Until that changes, the practical lesson is simple. Do not wait for the model on top of the leaderboard. Use the tools you can access, patch what attackers are already using, and plan your budget around cost per task rather than rank.
