items.title: Self-Retrospection Distillation Lifts AI Agent Success From 0% to 60.6% When Every Rollout Fails
items.author: Salesforce $CRM
items.content:
Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight

Haoxiang Zhang, Qinglin Chen, Hiroaki Hayashi, Zhuofeng Li, Siming Zhang, Jiaxin Zhang, Jixuan Chen, Fang Wu, Pan Lu, Silvio Savarese, Julian McAuley, Chien-Sheng Wu (Salesforce AI Research)

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce , which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to 24.2 pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when 37–98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In 2B setting, where 98% of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at 0.0% success, while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction. Code

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a scalable post-training paradigm for large language model (LLM) agents: by executing against automated verifiers and optimizing policies from outcome signals, it enables agents to develop complex, multi-step behavior without human-annotated traces (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). Applied to tool-integrated reasoning (Jin et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2025), code execution (Le et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2026), computer use (Wang et al., 2025a), and multi-agent coordination (Li et al., 2026; Ke et al., 2026), RLVR has proven remarkably effective in settings where agents must act in an external environment and learn from feedback revealed only through interaction.

The supervision in RLVR, however, is inherently retrospective: outcome signals become available only after interaction and are then assigned back to the actions that produced them. Yet a broad line of work on predictive control, world models, and planning suggests that effective interaction also depends on what an agent can anticipate before acting, how its interaction may fail, and what the environment is likely to demand (Pathak et al., 2017; Hafner et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2023). Such pre-interaction expectations shape subsequent exploration, but in RLVR they remain an implicit byproduct of optimizing behavior. More importantly, relying exclusively on post-hoc outcome contrast creates a fundamental blind spot: when all rollouts in a group receive the same reward, especially in long-horizon reasoning tasks where most attempts fail (Lightman et al., 2024), their group-relative advantages vanish (Schulman et al., 2017). The agent may have already revealed rich interactive information about the task and environment, yet learn no signal from that experience.

A recent line of on-policy self-distillation extracts a denser signal from this experience: a single model serves as both teacher and student, with the teacher conditioned on a privileged correct solution and the student trained to match its token-level distribution over the student’s own rollouts (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). Follow-ups vary what the privileged context contains — runtime feedback, skill summaries, or self-revisions — and hybrid objectives fold this signal back into RLVR (Wang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). Across these variants, however, the supervision target is unchanged: hindsight conditions the teacher to sharpen what the agent should do next. We ask instead what the agent could have known — whether the same completed experience can teach it to anticipate, before acting, the demands and failures that only interaction reveals.

We call this : hindsight supervises the agent’s foresight. Given a task, the agent predicts from pre-interaction information alone the knowledge the task may require and the failures it may invite, and the completed trajectory then provides privileged supervision for those predictions.

Building on this principle, we propose Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). For each on-policy trajectory, SRD pairs a pre-interaction prediction with a hindsight prediction conditioned on the completed interaction, and aligns their token-level distributions on the student’s own prospective rollout. As a result, every trajectory can contribute prospective supervision, precisely where reward contrast leaves none: on a failed rollout, the self-teacher’s hindsight lets the agent distill the mistake it just made into an anticipation it can carry forward, and on a saturated all-correct group, the same pairing keeps extracting the knowledge that made those rollouts succeed. Reward thus decides which lesson a trajectory teaches rather than whether it teaches one; learning then continues at both ends of the difficulty range that group-relative methods discard. We make three contributions:

  • A pre-interaction supervision target for agent experience. We formulate prospective learning (§3.1), a post-training target that distills structured information revealed after interaction into predictions constrained to the task and environment context available beforehand, complementary to the retrospective use of experience in RLVR and self-distillation.
  • A composable self-distillation instantiation. Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD, §3.2) adds a lightweight auxiliary objective to RLVR and self-distillation algorithms, and improves performance across diverse tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic settings (§4.2); our analysis characterizes the regimes in which this additional signal is most useful (§5).
  • Learning beyond scalar reward variance. SRD provides dense supervision from all trajectories and remains informative for reward-uniform baselines where RL yields zero advantage (§5).

We consider an agent policy πθ interacting with an environment . Given a task , the agent produces a trajectory τ=(a1,o1,…,aT,oT), where at∼πθ(⋅∣ht) is the action at step t, o_{t}\sim\mathcal{E}(\cdot\mid h_{t},a_{t}) the resulting observation, and ht the previous interaction history.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)

evaluates a completed trajectory with a verifier (e.g. a math checker, unit test, or task rubric), producing a scalar reward r(\tau)=\mathcal{V}(x,\tau) that is converted into an advantage estimate A⁡(τ) and assigned back to the actions that produced it:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RLVR}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Bigl[A(\tau)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\Bigr].

For group-relative methods such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), given G rollouts {τi}i=1G for the same task with rewards {ri}i=1G, the advantage is A⁡(τi)=(ri−μr)/σr, where μr and σr are the group mean and standard deviation. Critically, when all rollouts receive identical rewards, A⁡(τi)=0 for every i; standard practice discards such uniform-reward groups entirely and resamples until a discriminative batch is obtained (Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), prolonging the rollout and wasting trajectories and whatever information they contain.

Figure 1: Comparison of three paradigms for converting agent experience into training signals. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) scalarizes completed trajectories into outcome rewards and assigns them back to the action policy. Retrospective Learning retains structured post-hoc hindsight to supervise behavior. Prospective Learning uses hindsight to supervise predictions formed from information available before interaction.

Retrospective Learning from Agent Experience.

Beyond scalarizing a trajectory into an outcome, retrospective methods retain structured hindsight z^{\mathrm{hind}}=\mathcal{R}(x,\tau) extracted by a retrospection after interaction—encoding environment feedback, a selected solution, or a reusable skill. All such methods can be unified under a single objective: find a policy πθ that maximizes expected utility when the agent has access to hindsight derived from its own experience,

\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}_{z^{\mathrm{hind}}\sim\mathcal{R}(x,\tau)}\bigl[\mathcal{U}(\pi_{\theta},\,z^{\mathrm{hind}},\,x)\bigr]\Bigr],

where is a method-specific utility that measures how well the policy exploits the hindsight. RLVR is a degenerate instance in which zhind=r⁡(τ) is a scalar and reduces to the advantage-weighted log-likelihood. On-policy self-distillation (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026) sets zhind to a verified trace and to the negative Kullback-Leibler divergence between the hindsight-conditioned teacher and the student:

\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\pi_{\theta},z^{\mathrm{hind}},x)=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\Bigl(\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid h_{t},\,z^{\mathrm{hind}})\;\Big\|\;\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t})\Bigr),

where denotes the stop-gradient self-teacher, instantiated as the same model conditioned on privileged hindsight, and πθ the student conditioned only on the interaction history ht. Skill- and memory-based methods (Wang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026) extract reusable abstractions or reflections as zhind and optimize as downstream task performance.

Despite their differences, these retrospective methods share a common supervision target: post-hoc information is ultimately used to improve the agent’s reasoning or action policy. We next shift the supervision target from the agent takes to what the agent could have anticipated before interaction.

3 Learning Prospectively via Self-Retrospection Distillation

Retrospective learning (Objective 2) uses post-hoc experience zhind to supervise the agent’s reasoning or action policy. We formalize its complementary counterpart: let denote a structured prospection of what the upcoming interaction may unfold. Given a task x and its environment context e, we define the as

p_{\mathrm{fore}}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,e),

without access to the realized interaction. We suppress the specific prospection instruction from the notation; different instantiations may query different aspects of the upcoming interaction.

After interaction, the realized trajectory provides structured hindsight zhind, as defined in Section 2. Prospective learning utilizes this hindsight as privileged context to define a more informed distribution over the same output space:

p_{\mathrm{hind}}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,e,z^{\mathrm{hind}}),

where denotes a hindsight-conditioned teacher policy. Thus, pfore and phind differ in whether post-hoc interaction information is available. Prospective learning optimizes the foresight distribution to anticipate what hindsight reveals:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pro}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\;\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Bigl[D\bigl(p_{\mathrm{hind}}\;\|\;p_{\mathrm{fore}}\bigr)\Bigr].

Unlike retrospective objectives, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pro}} does not optimize the action distribution πθ(⋅∣ht) directly. It trains the agent to internalize, prior to interaction, the patterns of failure and knowledge that its own traces expose: a target remains informative as long as the agent’s anticipation lags behind what its own execution reveals.

Figure 2: Overview of Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). The student policy rolls out trajectories and generates anticipated pitfalls and knowledge foresights via a differently prompted call to the same model. Post-hoc experience from the completed trajectory conditions the stopped-gradient self-teacher, whose token-level distributions supervise the student’s own foresight rollout.

3.2 Self-Retrospection Distillation

We instantiate prospective learning as Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD) with two potential perspectives of foresight: Knowledge, describing knowledge that may be required during interaction, and Pitfall, describing failures that may be encountered. Both views follow the same distillation procedure and differ only in the prospection instruction used to query the model. Within an on-policy rollout group, successful trajectories provide Knowledge supervision, while failed trajectories provide Pitfall supervision, unifying positive and negative interaction experience as two sources of prospective supervision under the same objective. (Footnote: Detailed hindsight, foresight, pitfall, and knowledge prompts are provided in Appendix B.1.)

Hindsight and foresight construction.

For a task x, let {τi}i=1G denote its on-policy rollout group, with verified rewards {ri}. For each rollout i, we use ci to denote its prospective view—Knowledge when ri=1 and Pitfall when ri=0. Let fi=(τi,y∗,ϵi) denote its privileged post-hoc context, where y∗ refers to gold solution or ground-truth answer and ϵi is the corresponding error annotation when applicable. Conditioning on the same view ci, SRD defines a foresight distribution without access to the completed interaction and a hindsight-conditioned distribution that additionally observes fi:

p_{\mathrm{fore}}^{i}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,e,c^{i}),\qquad p_{\mathrm{hind}}^{i}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,e,f^{i},c^{i}).

Here, ci is shorthand for the corresponding prospection instruction. Thus, reward determines the of prospective supervision provided by a rollout, while foresight and hindsight within that view differ only in whether privileged post-hoc interaction information is available.

Hindsight-foresight alignment.

For each rollout, the student samples a foresight sequence zfore,i∼pforei. The hindsight teacher evaluates the same student-generated prefix with access to the post-hoc context fi. SRD minimizes token-level distillation loss over the rollout group:

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,\{\tau^{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{l=1}^{L_{i}}D\!\left(\pi_{\bar{\theta}}\!\left(\cdot\mid x,e,f^{i},z^{\mathrm{fore},i}_{<l}\right)\;\Big\|\;\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\cdot\mid x,e,z^{\mathrm{fore},i}_{<l}\right)\right)\right],

where D is any distribution divergence measure. A natural and stable choice is the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence, defined for β∈[0,1] as

\mathrm{JSD}_{\beta}(p_{T}\|p_{S})=\beta\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{T}\|m)+(1-\beta)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{S}\|m),\qquad m=\beta\,p_{T}+(1-\beta)\,p_{S},

where p_{T}=\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,e,f,\,z^{\mathrm{fore}}_{<l}) is the -teacher, instantiated as a stopped-gradient copy of the current policy, and pS=πθ(⋅∣x,e,z<lfore) the student.

SRD broadly improves post-training objectives and transfers beyond training conditions.

SRD improves category-level performance across GRPO, OPSD, and RLSD at both model scales, with only one regression—WebShop under 9B OPSD (−3.61 pp). The gains are often substantial. For 4B GRPO, adding SRD improves the Math, Code, and Search averages by 10.03, 8.33, and 8.05 pp, respectively, while also improving ALFWorld by 3.25 pp and WebShop by 5.92 pp. The effect extends to other optimization targets: at 9B, OPSD+SRD raises the Math average from 39.70% to 56.92% (+17.22 pp) and Search +10.31 pp. The gains extend to the hybrid objective: RLSD+SRD improves ALFWorld from 66.25% to 77.25% (+11.00 pp). These results indicate that SRD is not tied to a particular base objective, but complements pure RLVR, self-distillation, and their hybrid. The gains also persist when evaluation departs from the training interaction regime. On Code, where training uses the LCB format and evaluation uses functional-format problems, SRD improves the 4B GRPO average by 8.33 pp, including an 8.12 pp gain on OJBench. On the ALFWorld unseen environments, SRD improves every base-objective–scale combination, with gains ranging from 1.12 to 13.74 pp. BrowseComp-Plus further introduces a substantially longer interaction horizon (10× or more tool calls) than the training rollouts; SRD improves five of six settings there, by up to 9.52 pp.

SRD mitigates the instability of pure self-distillation.

Self-distillation without an outcome-grounded signal is the least stable baseline here, and its degradation is concentrated on several tool-integrated benchmarks. At 9B, OPSD alone ends up below the untrained policy — by 5.50 pp on HotpotQA, 3.76 pp on 2Wiki and 2.18 pp on LCB-v6 — i.e. the post-training run has spent its budget degrading the very interface it was supposed to sharpen. The symptom is visible in the scaling behaviour: the Math average of OPSD is across scale, the 9B run landing 2.11 pp the 4B one (39.70% vs. 41.81%), driven by AIME24 (54.17% vs. 62.50%) and AIME26 (52.92% vs. 54.17%). Adding SRD restores the expected ordering and improves both ends: OPSD+SRD reaches 48.11% at 4B and 56.92% at 9B, an 8.81 pp gap in the right direction, gaining 6.30 and 17.22 pp over the corresponding baseline, and all three Math benchmarks now scale monotonically (AIME24 +9.59, AIME26 +10.83, AMO +6.00 pp from 4B to 9B). The same repair shows on the three columns that had regressed below , which now stand at 10.75, 11.75 and 8.54 pp the untrained policy on HotpotQA, 2Wiki and LCB-v6, respectively. These results suggest that prospective supervision provides a complementary learning signal when direct hindsight-to-behavior distillation becomes unstable.

SRD remains effective as the base policy gets stronger.

The benefit of prospective supervision does not disappear at 9B: the best +SRD result increases from 4B to 9B in every task category, with particularly strong improvements in Math and Agentic tasks. Importantly, we observe that the gain from SRD does not increase monotonically with scale, but continues to provide complementary supervision even as the underlying policy becomes stronger. We examine why this signal persists across capability levels in dual-channel SRD in §5, where reward-uniform rollout groups remain prevalent despite a shift from predominantly all-failure to increasingly all-success groups.

In GRPO, a prompt contributes a non-zero policy-gradient signal only when its rollout group {τi}i=1G contains reward variation. To isolate this regime, we train on the code domain alone, disable dynamic sampling, and compare the same objective as Yu et al. (2025) with and without SRD across four Qwen3.5 scales (Figure Right). Reward-uniform groups consume a substantial fraction of the sampled budget across capability levels: the usable share of the budget never exceeds 63%, and the discarded share is in capability (98.0, 39.1, 37.0, 41.3 points), because as the policy strengthens all-zero reward groups fall monotonically (98.0→13.4) while all-one reward groups rise monotonically (0.0→27.9): a weak policy solves nothing, a strong one solves a lot, and neither leaves any outcome contrast to learn from. Appendix A.3 formalizes this pattern and shows how heterogeneity in prompt difficulty raises the uniform-group rate beyond the homogeneous prediction. Model scaling does not eliminate the blind spot, but it shifts it from failure saturation toward success saturation. Since \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} scores a trajectory against its own hindsight-conditioned prospection rather than against its peers, it needs no within-group reward variance and applies to every group. The 2B case is the limiting one: with 98% of groups uniform, the baseline’s reward is so sparse that it never gets off the ground (1.6% peak training success, 0.0% final), whereas the same budget with SRD reaches 60.6% in training.

As a training target a wrong foresight can be corrected by subsequent updates; spoken before acting, it conditions the whole episode. Generating it at inference is therefore not free.

RLVR learns from verifiable trajectory-level outcomes (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025), while process supervision raises the temporal resolution of that feedback (Lightman et al., 2024; Setlur et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025). A parallel line increases the information content retained from each completed rollout: on-policy self-distillation conditions a self-teacher on privileged solutions (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026), and its successors enrich that privileged context with self-revisions (He et al., 2026), trajectory-level skills (Wang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026), procedural memory (Liu et al., 2026), or an outcome-RL term (Yang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Recent diagnostics, however, show that enriching the teacher context is not unconditionally beneficial: privileged conditioning can alter calibration, self-correction, epistemic suppression, and even the teacher behavior being distilled (Zhang et al., 2026b; Kaur et al., 2026; Ichihara et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). These motivate separating two design choices that prior work conflates — and what hindsight supervises. Across all of the above, the supervision target is the same (the agent’s action distribution); SRD changes the target, redirecting hindsight from behavior to foresight.

Prospective Learning and Foresight.

Learning to anticipate the consequences of interaction has a long history in reinforcement learning. Early predictive and model-based methods learn from realized transitions to estimate future outcomes and support planning before execution (Sutton, 1988; Sutton, 1990), while later world-model approaches explicitly imagine possible futures — from learned “dreams” and latent dynamics to decision-relevant predictions used for planning (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2020; Schrittwieser et al., 2020). Complementary hindsight methods reuse realized outcomes to relabel or assign credit to past experience (Andrychowicz et al., 2017; Chelu et al., 2020). Recent language-agent work has brought these ideas closer together by learning action consequences, prospective state rollouts, and other forms of foresight before execution (Xie et al., 2025; Song et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2026c). SRD follows this predictive lineage but couples hindsight and foresight differently: completed interaction provides privileged training-time supervision for a trajectory-blind prediction of interaction-relevant structure. Thus, SRD does not require reconstructing a full future trajectory or explicitly consuming foresight for planning at inference time; hindsight teaches the shared policy what could have been anticipated before acting.

We introduced prospective learning, extending the use of post-hoc experience from behavioral revision to pre-interaction anticipation. Our proposed Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD) instantiates this principle by distilling hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight over interaction-relevant knowledge and failure modes. Empirically, SRD complements reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and self-distillation across diverse reasoning and agentic tasks, including regimes where objective-specific filtering leaves much of the sampled experience unused. More broadly, we view prospective learning as a post-training design axis, and we believe that a key direction toward more capable agents is to optimize not only how they learn from experience, but also how well they can anticipate what an interaction will demand and where it may fail before acting.

This work studies post-training for language-model agents on mathematical reasoning, programming, retrieval, and simulated interactive tasks. Improved task performance can also increase the effectiveness of agents used for harmful purposes, including unsafe code execution or unauthorized information access. Distilling a model’s own hindsight can reinforce errors and biases from its base model, training data, or feedback; benchmark gains therefore do not establish safety, fairness, or reliability in deployment. Applications beyond the evaluated settings should use task-specific safety evaluations, sandboxed execution, restricted tool permissions, and human oversight for consequential actions, with safeguards for sensitive information in interaction traces.

C.1 Training Data Construction

All methods and model scales use the same training examples in the same order. We first construct a source pool for each domain and then sample a fixed training mixture that is reused across all experimental arms.

We use DAPO-Math-17K (Yu et al., 2025) as the source pool and render each problem into our native multi-turn tool-calling format. Answers are graded by the DAPO rule-based verifier. AIME 2024, AIME 2026, and AMO-Bench are used only for evaluation and do not overlap with the training set.

The source pool consists of the and problems from the portion of LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), yielding 2,000 candidate training prompts. Evaluation uses held-out problems in the functional Python format of LCB-v6 together with OJBench (Wang et al., 2025b). Training and evaluation therefore differ both in problem instances and submission format. A submission is marked correct only if it passes all retained unit tests.

Following Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025a), we construct a source pool from 1,500 training questions each from HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, obtained through FlashRAG (Jin et al., 2025b). The agent interacts with a fixed search interface backed by a local BM25 index over Wikipedia-18. Held-out development questions from HotpotQA and 2Wiki are used for evaluation, while BrowseComp-Plus is never used for training.

For ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), we train on the 400 games from the standard TextWorld training split and evaluate on 100 out-of-distribution games with unseen room layouts and object placements, while preserving all chat histories. For WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), we follow the standard session partition used by Xia et al. (2026), using 400 training and 100 held-out shopping instructions. Success requires the environment to return a terminal score of 1.0.

For Math, Code, and Search, each run uses a fixed equal-ratio mixture of all prompts per domain, shuffled once and reused in the same order for every method and model scale. ALFWorld and WebShop are jointly trained in a second mixture with 1:1 prompts from each environment. This controls the training data and ordering across all compared objectives.

We train Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B with thinking-on on a single node with 8× NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each training step samples 16 prompts with 8 on-policy rollouts per prompt, giving 128 trajectories before dynamic-sampling resampling. We keep the nominal step count and retained batch size fixed across comparable arms so that methods are trained with the same number of accepted trajectories per optimization step.

  • keeps a prompt group only if its rewards have non-zero standard deviation. An all-correct or all-incorrect group has a vanishing group-relative advantage for every token it contains and contributes exactly zero gradient, so retaining it would consume batch capacity without moving the policy.

The asymmetry matters for interpreting the results. The two filters accept different sets of groups, so the two families pay different rollout costs to fill an identical batch, and the groups that RLVR must throw away (all-correct and all-incorrect) are precisely the ones where an outcome-reward contrast carries no information. This is why we also report a variant with dynamic sampling in §5, in which every sampled group is trained on regardless of its reward pattern: SRD continues to learn from the groups the filters would have discarded, which is the most direct expression of its sample efficiency.

C.5 Evaluation Benchmarks and Protocol

Unless otherwise specified, we evaluate each checkpoint with avg​@​8: for every prompt, we sample 8 independent trajectories at temperature 1.0 and topp=1.0, compute the fraction of successful trajectories, and then average across evaluation prompts. All compared methods use the same fixed evaluation sets and task interfaces. For math/code/search, we set max output per turn as 16K; in agentic tasks, we set this as 8K. Math answers are graded by the DAPO verifier, search answers by exact match, code by execution against retained unit tests, and the agentic environments by their native binary success signals; for additional LLM-as-judge fallback, please refer to §B.2.

We evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AIME 2026 (Art of Problem Solving, 2026), and AMO-Bench (An et al., 2025). AIME 24, 25, and 26 each contain 30 olympiad-level problems with automatically verifiable integer answers. AIME 2026 postdates the backbone’s pretraining cutoff and therefore provides a more contamination-resistant evaluation. AMO-Bench contains 50 harder olympiad-style problems with verifiable short answers and serves as our most challenging mathematical reasoning benchmark.

We evaluate on the functional Python split of LiveCodeBench-v6 (Jain et al., 2025) (63 problems) and the medium-difficulty Python track of OJBench (Wang et al., 2025b). This differs from training, which uses the format of LiveCodeBench, and therefore tests transfer across both problem instances and submission formats. The graded candidate is the final program executed by the agent through the interpreter rather than the last fenced code block in its response. A problem receives credit only when the executed program passes all retained unit tests; partial credit is not awarded. We retain at most 10 tests per LCB problem and 15 per OJBench problem, with a 6-second limit per test. After filtering problems with unavailable upstream test data or unsupported inputs, the OJBench evaluation set contains 77 problems (52 NOI and 25 ICPC).

We evaluate short-horizon retrieval on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020), and long-horizon evidence gathering on BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025). For HotpotQA and 2Wiki, we construct fixed 100-question evaluation subsets from their held-out development splits using Qwen3-8B under the Search-R1 scaffold as a difficulty calibrator. We retain questions whose empirical pass​@​8 lies above 0% but below 30%, avoiding examples that are nearly always solved or nearly always failed by the reference policy or incorrect/blur ground truth answers. The resulting subsets are fixed once and reused unchanged across all methods and model scales.

HotpotQA and 2Wiki use the same local retrieval interface as training, with answers graded by exact match. BrowseComp-Plus is never used for training and evaluates substantially longer-horizon evidence gathering with the fixed tool setting of Zhang et al. (2026a). It is evaluated with its dedicated benchmark harness rather than the standard short-horizon Search-R1 scaffold.

ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) evaluates on the standard out-of-distribution split of 100 games, whose room layouts and object placements are unseen during training. WebShop (Yao et al., 2022) uses 100 held-out shopping sessions under the standard session partition. An episode is counted as successful only when the environment returns its terminal success criterion; for WebShop, this requires an exact match to the requested product attributes and options.

E.4 Why SRD Lengthens the RL Step and Shortens the Self-Distillation One

The two families move in opposite directions when \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} is added: 0.39→0.86 for GRPO but 1.97→0.57 for OPSD. Three measured facts make this less surprising than it first reads.

First, the two hosts are not comparable to begin with. Self-distillation supplies a dense per-token target at every position, whereas GRPO supplies one sparse advantage per trajectory under a KL leash to the base, so the self-distillation run ends up ∥S∥/∥A∥=5.1× further from the base. The question is therefore not why one grew and the other shrank, but why both ended up at a distance: ∥E∥=0.86 against ∥ES∥=0.57, a factor of 1.5, where their hosts differed by a factor of 5.

Second, the shrinkage in the OPSD family is pure shrinkage, not redirection. Projecting ES onto gives αES/∥S∥=0.278 with only 0.194 of ES off that axis, i.e. ES≈0.28​S: the same ray, a shorter distance. That is the signature of an added regulariser or an earlier stop, not of a competing objective. The growth in the GRPO family has the opposite signature: α/∥A∥=1.30 an orthogonal component of comparable size (0.493 of ∥E∥), i.e. further along the same axis and also into a direction GRPO does not travel in.

Third, this is what the term is: \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} is a dense per-token divergence to a prospection target derived from the policy itself. Against a host that provides no dense signal, it is the only such signal, and it adds movement. Against a host that is already a dense self-distillation, it is a self-referential target — prospection without the hindsight block — competing for the same capacity, and it behaves like an anchor: the run travels less far along the direction it was already going.

We flag the limitation this reading rests on. These are displacements of the final checkpoint from the base, so they conflate the size of a step with the number of effective steps; the two runs in each pair share hyperparameters but not the total loss, and we measure only the endpoint. Repeating the same norms at intermediate checkpoints would separate the two, and we have not done that.

An earlier trial analyzed that the SRD update was anti-aligned with the RL update, from cos⁡(F−A,A) with A=log⁡pGRPO−log⁡pbase and F=log⁡pGRPO+SRD−log⁡pbase. That statistic cannot be positive: the two arguments share the term A, which forces

The blind foresight gets the shape of the problem right and the location of the constraint wrong, which is the most informative way it could fail. Its second block correctly anticipates that a two-object task has a capacity problem, and then places that capacity on the : it asks whether can hold two cards, and advises hunting for a second armchair if not. The real limit is on the — one carried object at a time — and it is enforced by withdrawing every from the admissible list the instant the first card is in hand. No observation states the rule in words; it is disclosed only implicitly, as a change in the action set between the empty-handed and holding states, and the agent has to induce the constraint from that difference. The failing rollout registers the difference — it reads the list and notes the action is absent — but cannot make the inference, and concludes only that the situation is “strange”.

That asymmetry is what the Pitfall channel is being asked to close here. The hindsight states the rule in the environment’s own terms — admissible actions change from ‘‘take’’ to ‘‘move’’ based on inventory state — and pairs it with the ordering that follows: place before you collect again. Neither the task string (put two creditcard in armchair) nor the tool schema contains that fact. Seven of the eight rollouts fail under the zero-slack budget, and they fail in two distinguishable ways: four spend it sweeping receptacle classes that never held the cards, while three reach both cards and are stopped by the carry constraint they could not have known.

F.4 All-Success Groups and the Knowledge Channel

A group in which every rollout succeeds is reward-uniform for the same structural reason as an all-fail group: , the advantage vanishes for every token, and a group-relative objective learns nothing from it. It is also the half of the construction that the Pitfall channel cannot serve, since there is no failure to diagnose. The group below is drawn from the run in which both channels are distilled and the Knowledge student is blind to the solution.

Example from # DAPO-Math — an all-success group

Problem. Suppose that x, y, z are positive reals satisfying

Then can be expressed as mn with m,n coprime positive integers. Compute m+n.

Group outcome. r⁡(τi)=1 for all i=1,…,8; tool calls per rollout [2,5,1,2,2,4,3,2].

What the student prospects.

The Knowledge foresights for this group, sampled independently from the problem alone. They agree: all read the a2+a​b+b2 form as a 120∘ Law of Cosines and propose the Fermat-point construction.

Knowledge foresight zfore — rollout A

[Knowledge/Rule] A rule for decoding cyclic systems with quadratic forms resembling the Law of Cosines. Many equations involving three variables in cyclic quadratics (e.g. a2+a​b+b2=C) correspond to the Law of Cosines in triangles with a fixed internal angle of 120∘ (cos⁡120∘=−12). Treating x,y,z as side lengths from a common point O, the system implies that they form the sides of a triangle with a 120∘ angle between each adjacent pair when arranged around a central point. [Details/Examples] Constructing a figure where O​A=x, O​B=y, O​C=z meet at 120∘ angles allows one to compute the sides of triangle A​B​C from the given constants. The area can then be calculated two ways — as the sum of three smaller 120∘ triangles, and by a standard side-area formula — to relate x​y​z to the constants.

Knowledge foresight zfore — rollout B

[Knowledge/Rule] Recognizing algebraic structures based on the Law of Cosines, where a system involving three pairs of variables matching the form a2+a​b+b2=k represents the squared side lengths of triangles with angles of 120∘. [Details/Examples] The equation a2+a​b+b2=c2 represents a triangle with sides a, b, c where the angle opposite c is 120∘. If three such equations form a cycle for x,y,z, they can be visualized as three sides of a larger triangle containing a central point where the pairwise angles are all 120∘.

[Knowledge/Rule] Using Ptolemy’s Theorem or coordinate geometry to relate the geometry of a cyclic quadrilateral (or the specific 120∘ configuration) to the product of the legs of the component triangles, often leading to a calculation involving the area or specific side lengths of the constructed larger triangle. [Details/Examples] If x,y,z are sides of triangles with a common 120∘ vertex joined cyclically, the outer triangle’s side lengths satisfy L_{x}=\sqrt{y^{2}+yz+z^{2}}, etc. The system implies x,y,z correspond to segments forming a larger triangle with sides \sqrt{64}=8, \sqrt{49}=7, \sqrt{57}. One can use the area of this larger triangle, or direct algebraic relations from the cosine law, to find x​y​z.

[Knowledge/Rule] Applying principles of symmetric systems, or algebraic identities for cyclic x2+x​y+y2 sums, to extract the product x​y​z without solving for individual variables — often using the relationship between the area of the outer triangle and the areas of the inner sub-triangles. [Details/Examples] A common technique involves realizing the outer triangle is constructible and using Heron’s formula or vector algebra to isolate the term under the cube root.

What the trajectories actually did.

The anticipation is stable; the realizations are not. Across the eight correct rollouts we find at least three distinct routes, two of which are shown below.

Trajectory A — exact symbolic elimination (1 tool call)

Reasoning Content: These equations look similar to the law of cosines […] x2+y2−2​x​y​cos⁡(120∘), since cos(120∘)=−1/2. So this suggests we could think of these as distances in a triangle with 120∘ angles.

Actually, let me try a different approach. […] Let me subtract equations to find relationships between the variables.

⬇
from sympy import symbols, solve, Eq

x, y, z = symbols(’x y z’, positive=True, real=True)

solution = solve((Eq(x**2 + x*y + y**2, 64),

                  Eq(y**2 + y*z + z**2, 49),

                  Eq(z**2 + z*x + x**2, 57)), (x, y, z))

Solutions: [(64/13, 56/13, 49/13)] xyz: 175616/2197

Final Answer. Subtracting pairs gives (x−z)​S=15, (y−x)​S=−8, (z−y)​S=−7 with S=x+y+z; substituting into x+y+z=S yields x=S/3+23/(3​S), y=S/3−1/(3​S), z=S/3−22/(3​S), and the first equation then forces S2=169 or S2=1. Positivity selects S=13, so and m+n=69. The geometry is never used.

Trajectory B — geometric reading, then numeric solve and rational reconstruction (2 tool calls)

Reasoning Content: x2+xy+y2=x2+y2−2xy(−1/2), so this corresponds to cosC=−1/2, which means C=120∘. So if we imagine a point O and three points A,B,C such that O​A=x, O​B=y, ∠​A​O​B=120∘, then A​B2=x2+y2+x​y=64, so A​B=8; likewise B​C=7 and. The angles around O sum to 360∘ […]

— numeric solve from several initial guesses.

⬇
solutions = sympy.nsolve((eq1, eq2, eq3), (x, y, z), (5, 4, 3))

for guess in [(6, 4, 3), (5, 5, 4), (4, 6, 3), (4, 4, 5)]:

    sol = sympy.nsolve((eq1, eq2, eq3), (x, y, z), guess)

⬇
Numerical solution: Matrix([[4.92307692307692],

                           [4.30769230769231],

                           [3.76923076923077]])

recognises \sqrt[3]{xyz}\approx 4.30769\approx 56/13, conjectures (x,y,z)=(64/13,56/13,49/13), and verifies those rationals exactly against all three equations.

, so m+n=69.

One anticipation, many realizations.

A third rollout parametrises directly by S, solves x2+x​y+y2=64 for S∈{1,13}, and rejects S=1 on the grounds that it forces y=0 and z=−7. So the group contains an exact algebraic elimination, a numeric solve with rational reconstruction, and a parametrise-then-prune argument — all reaching 56/13, none of them the area double-count that every foresight proposed.

This is the sense in which the Knowledge channel is not a request for method. The teacher for each rollout is privileged with that rollout’s own trajectory, so the same stable anticipation is paired with three different realizations, and \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SRD}} pulls the prediction toward the route that rollout actually had available rather than toward a canonical solution. The diversity is the asset: a group that a group-relative objective sees as eight identical zeros of advantage is, to a prospective objective, eight different demonstrations of what this problem admits.

F.5 How Each Channel’s Foresight Changes over Training

This section asks a different question: conditional on a channel, does the of the prediction change? To avoid confounding the answer with the shifting domain mix, we hold the domain fixed to mathematics and compare early against late records of each channel in the dual-channel run.

Knowledge: from a single identity to a solution strategy.

The two problems compared are both algebraic-system questions from DAPO-Math.

Step 1. The numbers 11,12,…,12010 are written on a blackboard. A student chooses any two of the numbers, say x and y, erases them, and then writes down x+y+x​y. He continues this process until only one number is left on the blackboard. What is this number?

Step 45. Suppose w,x,y,z satisfy

The largest possible value of w can be expressed in lowest terms as w1w2 for integers w1,w2>0. Find w1+w2.

Early Knowledge foresights tend to name one transferable fact and stop. The step-1 example is a good one — it spots the substitution that linearises the whole problem — but it is a single observation.

Knowledge foresight — step 1

[Knowledge/Rule] The operation x∘y=x+y+x​y is associative and commutative, meaning the final result depends only on the set of initial numbers, not the order of operations. This operation is isomorphic to standard multiplication via the transformation f⁡(z)=z+1. [Details/Examples] Transform the operation by letting a′=a+1. Then the new operation on primed values becomes a′∘′b′=a′​b′. Thus iterating x∘y on the original numbers is equivalent to multiplying their (value+1) counterparts. For example, applying the rule to {1,2}: (1∘2)+1=6, which equals (1+1)​(2+1)=6.

Late Knowledge foresights more often lay out a : several facts ordered so that each one licenses the next.

Knowledge foresight — step 45

[Knowledge/Rule] Vieta’s formulas for quadratic roots. A polynomial t2−(sum)​t+(product)=0 has roots whose sum is the coefficient of t with opposite sign. This allows grouping variables into quadratic equations when a sum and product relationship are known. [Details/Examples] If a+b=S and a​b=P, they are the roots of t2−S​t+P=0. If a+b=5 and a​b=6, then t2−5​t+6=0 gives t=2,3.

[Knowledge/Rule] Non-existence of real roots. A quadratic a​t2+b​t+c=0 with real coefficients has no real solutions iff its discriminant Δ=b2−4​a​c is negative; equal real roots occur at Δ=0. [Details/Examples] For t2−4​t+5=0, Δ=16−20=−4<0, so no real t satisfies it.

[Knowledge/Rule] Optimisation of one variable under real-solvability constraints. To maximise w where x,y,z must remain real, eliminate the secondary variables to form an inequality in w. The boundary of the feasible region occurs when the auxiliary quadratic has a repeated real root, i.e. when its discriminant is exactly zero. [Details/Examples] Express the constraint as a quadratic in one variable and require Δ≥0; the extremum sits at Δ=0.

The three blocks are not independent facts: Vieta turns the symmetric constraints into a quadratic, the discriminant condition turns “the other variables are real” into an inequality, and the third block says where in that inequality the optimum lies. That composition is what is absent from the step-1 example, which states its identity and stops.

Pitfall: from generic procedure to problem-structure traps.

The two problems compared are both algebraic-system questions from DAPO-Math.

Step 0. Determine the real number a such that f⁡(a)=a is a relative minimum of the function f⁡(x)=x4−x3−x2+a​x+1.

Step 47. Find the sum of all positive integers n such that 2​n+1n⁡(n−1) has a terminating decimal representation.

The early Pitfall foresights read like exam advice — correct, but about the method in general rather than about this problem.

Pitfall foresight — step 0

[Error] Confusing the definition of “absolute” minimum with “relative” (local) minimum, or assuming the critical point at x=a must be the global minimum of the function on \mathbb{R}. [Rule] Apply the second-derivative test to classify critical points locally, without evaluating global behaviour unless explicitly required. For f⁡(x), check whether f′′​(a)>0 for a relative minimum. [Example] For f⁡(x)=x2, the critical point x=0 is a relative minimum because f′′​(0)=2>0, even though it is also the absolute minimum.

Later ones more often name a trap that exists only because of how expression is built.

Pitfall foresight — step 47

[Error] Overlooking the factor of n−1 in the denominator when reducing the fraction. Since the expression is (2​n+1)/(n⁡(n−1)), the denominator is n⁡(n−1). A solver might only check the prime factors of n and ignore (n−1), leading to false positives. [Rule] To ensure the reduced denominator is of the form 2a​5b, both factors of the unreduced denominator, n and (n−1), must contribute only the primes 2 and 5 after cancelling any common factors with the numerator (2​n+1). [Example] For n=4: denominator 4⋅3=12, numerator 9, fraction 9/12=3/4, denominator 22 — valid. For n=3: denominator 3⋅2=6, numerator 7, fraction 7/6, denominator has a factor 3 — invalid.

items.title: SpaceX Teams Up With Qualcomm to Build a Nationwide 5G Network
items.author: Bruce Li
items.content:
The company that put thousands of routers in orbit is now coming down to earth: steel towers, rooftop leases, zoning boards and all. Here's what's planned, how 5G works, and why the hard part isn't the rockets.

Back in February 2020, I wrote a parody called "SpaceX Starlink Master Plan", in the voice of a certain CEO. It copied the "trickle-down" structure of Tesla's master plan, in four steps:

  1. Build a bulky, expensive terminal for professionals.
  2. Use that money to build a rooftop consumer terminal.
  3. Use that money to build "a low cost and high volume mobile phone."
  4. Build an interstellar communication system for Mars and beyond.

Fake-Elon also bragged that Starlink could beat 5G because the carriers "need to deploy a lot more cell sites," while Starlink doesn't "need to pay site rentals and backhaul." For the astronomers, he promised to paint every satellite chroma green "so they can be easily removed in photoshop."

Six and a half years later, steps 1 and 2 happened, if not quite in that order (consumers came first): millions of pizza-box dishes, on roofs and on boats. Step 3 took a turn I didn't see coming. SpaceX never built a StarPhone; it made phone a StarPhone, beaming signals straight to the one already in your pocket. And now comes the twist the parody never imagined: SpaceX is about to pay site rentals. Lots of them.

For about 30 years, American mobile service has worked like this: three giant companies own the networks (the airwaves, the radios bolted to the towers, and your monthly bill), and everyone else rents from them. Not even the giants own most of the towers anymore. Over a decade ago they sold or long-term leased them to landlords like American Tower and Crown Castle, and now pay rent like everybody else. Upstarts have tried to break in. Most have ended up as footnotes, or as a Boost Mobile ad.

Now a rocket company wants a go. On November 4, 2026, SpaceX and Qualcomm announced a multi-year deal under which Qualcomm supplies the core radio silicon and software for a nationwide terrestrial 5G network under the Starlink Mobile brand. SpaceX already has phone service coming from orbit. This time the plan is phone service coming , from tens of thousands of ordinary cell sites. Construction starts in 2027; when you can actually get service from them, nobody has said.

So: what exactly was announced, how does the technology work, and how many billions of dollars and zoning hearings stand between SpaceX and your SIM card?

1. The Announcement: Starlink Gets a Ground Game

  • Qualcomm supplies the guts of the radio access network (RAN): the radio-unit and baseband platforms (chips plus reference designs) and the commercial-grade Layer 1 software, all from its cellular infrastructure line. SpaceX builds the actual boxes around them. Neither company disclosed the dollar value.
  • "Tens of thousands of sites," according to the announcement, and Qualcomm executive vice president Durga Malladi expects the rollout to "ramp up pretty rapidly." Unconfirmed press reports say SpaceX is talking to tower owners about access to as many as ; no tower partners have been named.
  • Tower deployment starts in 2027. No launch date for terrestrial service has been given. Separately, SpaceX is targeting to switch on its next-generation "full 5G quality" service.
  • a genuine fourth national carrier that owns its own network, not just another reseller.

Malladi called it "huge," and agreed with Light Reading that it's Qualcomm's biggest network deal since 3G. For a company best known for the modem in your phone, that's a big deal.

Dragonwing, launched in February 2025, is Qualcomm's brand for its industrial, networking and infrastructure silicon, the chips that go into things other than phones.

The Dragonwing toolbox (the deal announcement names the QRU100 and QDU100 platforms specifically):

Radio unit platform supporting massive MIMO (64 transmit, 64 receive paths)

Up on the tower, behind the antenna

Distributed-unit Layer 1 baseband platform; its card form, the X100, is an inline PCIe accelerator (35 W max) that slots into ordinary Dell or HPE servers

In a cabinet at the base of the tower or a nearby edge site

The RF transceiver chips that turn bits into radio waves and back

AI features + RAN Automation Suite

AI beam prediction, uplink tuning and factory calibration built into the platforms, plus a separate network-management suite

Everywhere, apparently, because it's 2026

This gear has been deployed before, though not at this scale. Vietnam's runs Qualcomm-based radios across "a few thousand sites," and Qualcomm chips have shown up inside radios from NEC and Mavenir (which has since quit making radios). SpaceX is about to become its first customer at continental scale.

Qualcomm handles the physical layer, the hard real-time signal math. SpaceX is expected to write its own Layer 2, Layer 3 and core network software on top. As Malladi put it, "They still have to do the Layer 2, the Layer 3, and so on." That's very SpaceX: buy the chips and own the software, the same way it treats rocket engines and satellite buses.

The airwaves SpaceX has lined up

Radios are useless without airwaves, and in about 13 months SpaceX has agreed to spend roughly on spectrum (not all of it paid yet):

  • EchoStar (September 2025): about 50 MHz of 2 GHz AWS-4 and H-Block spectrum for about $17 billion (half cash, half SpaceX stock), plus roughly $2 billion of EchoStar's debt interest. In November 2025 SpaceX added a 15 MHz uplink-only AWS-3 slice (1695–1710 MHz) for about $2.6 billion in stock, for a total of roughly . The FCC approved the deal in May 2026 and allowed the spectrum to be used from space, on the ground, or both, which SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen calls crucial. The final closing, when SpaceX actually pays, is expected around late 2027.
  • Grain Management (October 2026): up to 14 MHz of paired, nationwide low-band spectrum for a reported (terms undisclosed; FCC approval pending). These airwaves started life at Nextel, passed to Sprint and then T-Mobile, which sold them to private investor Grain for about $3.6 billion ($2.9 billion in cash plus Grain's 600 MHz licenses) in a deal that closed in August 2026. Grain flipped them to SpaceX two months later for more than double that, which suggests either very good timing or a buyer in a hurry.

SpaceX is also reportedly (per the ) in talks to buy from EchoStar. That would bring an existing customer base, retail distribution, and wholesale roaming deals with AT&T and T-Mobile, two carriers that have so far shown little interest in signing anything directly with Elon Musk.

2. The State of American Wireless: Three Giants and a Rounding Error

The U.S. market is a mature three-way oligopoly. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile together serve the overwhelming majority of American phone lines, each with roughly 120 to 147 million connections. Cable companies (Comcast's Xfinity Mobile, Charter's Spectrum Mobile, about 23 million lines combined) have become the fastest-growing challengers, but they cheat a little: their consumer service runs on Verizon's network as an MVNO, and they push as much traffic as possible onto their own Wi-Fi (plus some CBRS small cells).

  • the 5G speed leader, thanks to Sprint's mid-band spectrum. It holds "nearly 400 MHz" of airwaves. Remember that number.
  • the coverage champ, finally growing again (406,000 postpaid phone adds in Q3 2026).
  • betting on fiber-plus-wireless bundles, and swapping its Nokia gear for Ericsson's.

AT&T and Verizon each plan to spend $16–24 billion on their networks in 2026, and T-Mobile about $10 billion. That's the annual fee for staying in this business.

Pay more, get… about the same

A three-way oligopoly is a comfortable place to be, if you're one of the three. Americans pay some of the highest mobile prices in the developed world:

Avg. mobile revenue per user, per month (2023)

Major mobile network operators

Typically 3–4 per country

Source: Connect Europe, State of Digital Communications 2025.

Notably, South Korea also has just three carriers and still charges far less, so the number of players isn't the whole story. Scale, geography and decades of regulatory choices all play a part.

That pricing turns into money. The Big Three post EBITDA margins in the mid-30s percent, which makes them some of the most profitable mobile operators anywhere. European carriers, squeezed by cutthroat competition, have spent the past decade complaining about the opposite problem.

What do Americans get for the premium? A good network, but not a world-beating one. Opensignal's Global Network Excellence Index ranked the U.S. in the world in late 2025, behind South Korea, among others. Ookla's Speedtest index has put U.S. median mobile download speeds somewhere between 9th and 13th in recent months, far behind the Gulf states and South Korea. And the rural dead zones are still there. In fairness, covering a huge, sparsely populated continent costs more than wiring Seoul. But that gap between price and performance is exactly the opening a fourth carrier is looking for.

The cautionary tale named Dish

The last company to try building a fourth facilities-based network was Dish (later EchoStar). Regulators made it the designated fourth carrier as a condition of the T-Mobile–Sprint merger, which closed in 2020. It built what it billed as the world's first cloud-native Open RAN 5G network and hit its 2023 coverage milestone of 70% of the population (its later deadline was pushed back). Then in 2025 it agreed to sell its spectrum to AT&T and SpaceX, and it is now moving Boost customers onto AT&T's network as a hybrid MVNO. Its wireless unit filed for Chapter 11 in mid-2026.

So the most recent attempt to build a new U.S. carrier ended with a handful of companies dividing up its airwaves, and SpaceX was one of the buyers.

Where Starlink 5G could fit

SpaceX isn't going to out-Verizon Verizon in midtown Manhattan in 2028. It's going after the problems the incumbents have never fully solved:

  1. Highways through the Mojave, national parks, farmland, the stretch of interstate where your podcast always cuts out. The carriers' coverage maps are generous, and the reality is patchier. Towers rarely pay for themselves out there; SpaceX's satellites can cover those gaps without them.
  2. Seamless ground-to-space handoff. Today, satellite texting from T-Mobile's T-Satellite or Apple's Globalstar-based service (Amazon is buying Globalstar) is a separate, slower mode you drop into. SpaceX wants a single network where your phone moves from tower to satellite and back without you noticing.
  3. Starlink already rattled the broadband market. A carrier with no legacy network and no union-negotiated copper plant to maintain could undercut the incumbents on price, or charge a premium for "never lose signal."

The incumbents, for their part, sound unbothered. "The physics just don't allow direct-to-cell to be a substitute product," said T-Mobile's (outgoing) CFO Peter Osvaldik in September. Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said Starlink "just can't compete without a terrestrial network in urban and suburban." Hence the towers.

3. A Primer on Cellular, 5G, and Phones That Talk to Space

Cellular in one paragraph

A cellular network divides the world into , areas each served by a base station. Your phone talks to the nearest one over licensed radio spectrum. The base station passes your data back over (fiber, or a microwave radio link) to the operator's , which handles authentication, billing, mobility, and the connection to the internet. When you move, the network hands you off to the next cell. Every generation since the 1980s (1G analog voice, 2G digital voice and SMS, 3G mobile data, 4G LTE mobile broadband, 5G) has been a better trick for packing more bits into the same air.

What actually makes 5G faster

5G New Radio (NR) isn't magic. It uses three broad levers:

1. More spectrum, in three flavors. Radio physics forces a trade-off: lower frequencies travel farther and go through walls, while higher frequencies carry more data but give up at the first pane of low-E glass.

  • the coverage layer. Goes for miles and works deep indoors. Spectrum is scarce, so channels are narrow. SpaceX's 800 MHz lives here.
  • Mid-band (roughly 1–7 GHz): the "Goldilocks" layer, a usable mix of reach and capacity. This is where 5G mostly lives. SpaceX's 2 GHz AWS-4 lives here.
  • High-band / mmWave (24 GHz+): blazing fast, with a range of about a city block, and blocked by leaves, rain, and your own hand. Mostly found in stadiums and press releases.

Every radio symbol encodes bits through combinations of amplitude and phase. Since 3GPP Release 17, 5G's downlink supports up to , meaning 10 bits per symbol, but only when the signal is clean enough. It's like a crowded restaurant: the quieter the room, the faster you can talk.

3. Massive MIMO and beamforming. This is the big one. An old 4G antenna is a floodlight: it sprays energy across a whole 120° sector. A 5G panel such as Qualcomm's 64T64R has dozens of small antenna elements. By adjusting the phase of each element's signal, the base station makes the waves add up in some directions and cancel in others. That produces focused aimed at individual phones.

Once you can aim beams, you can reuse the same frequencies for several users at the same time, as long as they're in different places. This is . Vendor and industry estimates suggest a 64T64R sector can carry roughly of a 4T4R sector on the same 100 MHz, and give users at the cell edge a signal boost of around 9 dB.

There's a catch that matters a lot for SpaceX. Most massive MIMO deployments use spectrum, where uplink and downlink take turns on the same channel, which makes it easy for the base station to learn the radio channel. SpaceX's spectrum is all : paired blocks with separate uplink and downlink channels, plus an uplink-only slice, and no TDD at all. Massive MIMO is harder to do well on FDD, and the FDD deployments out there today are mostly 32T32R. "If they're spectrum constrained, which they are, then this FDD massive MIMO is the way to get the capacity but especially the coverage benefits," says Omdia analyst Gabriel Brown. Qualcomm's pitch is that it can make 64T64R work well on SpaceX's 2 GHz FDD bands. A lot depends on that being true.

Plus the 5G stuff you've heard about. A standalone 5G core makes possible (virtual private networks with guaranteed performance), lower latency, and better handling of huge numbers of IoT devices. These matter for enterprises and are mostly invisible to people scrolling TikTok.

Now contrast that with a cell tower in orbit

SpaceX's existing satellites (about 650 launched since January 2024) work on a seemingly impossible premise: talk to an smartphone from hundreds of kilometers up.

Here is what they're up against:

~350–550 km (and more at an angle)

Still ~0.2 W. Your phone didn't get stronger

A beam tens of kilometers wide

Potentially thousands (illustrative)

Mostly no; you need sky view

None; the tower stays put

Satellite moves at ~7.6 km/s and the network must handle Doppler shift and constant handoffs

Texts, low-rate data, some apps

The satellites make up for it with brute force: huge phased-array antennas (several square meters) and very sensitive receivers, so they can pick up a phone's faint signal from orbit. Each satellite is essentially an eNodeB (an LTE base station) in space, backhauled through laser links to the rest of Starlink. That's the clever part. The phone thinks it's talking to an unusually distant tower in a roaming partner's network.

SpaceX's next-generation satellites, dubbed Starlink Mobile V2 and borrowing technology from its V3 broadband satellites, start launching on Starship around mid-2027. In October 2026 the FCC authorized a constellation of up to 15,000 of them. CFO Johnsen promises a "full 5G quality service," and SpaceX's target is up to 150 Mbps per user at peak. New 3GPP Release 19 phone modems with built-in satellite support, like Qualcomm's X105, should help. Even so, physics has a vote. A satellite beam covering a whole county is one shared cell. It will never match the capacity of a dense mesh of towers in a city.

That's the whole logic of the terrestrial plan: towers for capacity, satellites for coverage, one network for both.

The traditional cartel… er, "ecosystem"

Global RAN equipment is one of the most concentrated markets in tech. According to Dell'Oro and Omdia, the top five vendors (Huawei, Ericsson, Nokia, ZTE and Samsung) took about 95–96% of RAN revenue in 2025, and Dell'Oro says market concentration hit a ten-year high.

  • the global #1. Together with Ericsson, it holds nearly two-thirds of the market. Huawei is also banned from U.S. networks for national security reasons, and rural carriers are still working through a federally funded "rip and replace" program to remove its gear (fully funded since 2025, about half done).
  • the U.S. heavyweight, with more than 60% of North American RAN. In December 2023 it won AT&T's Open RAN contract, worth up to $14 billion. Ericsson is the vendor you hire when you want nobody to get fired.
  • #3 globally, T-Mobile's other main RAN supplier, which lost AT&T to Ericsson. It got a lifeline from NVIDIA in October 2025: a $1 billion investment to develop GPU-based "AI-RAN."
  • the other Chinese giant, also effectively shut out of the U.S.
  • the top challenger in the U.S., with a $6.6 billion Verizon contract and virtualized RAN software that runs on standard servers. It also supplied part of Dish's network.

The traditional model was : the radio on the tower and the baseband box at the bottom came from the same vendor and spoke a proprietary dialect over the cable between them. Once you'd picked Ericsson, you were an Ericsson shop for a decade.

Open RAN cracks the box open

(driven by the O-RAN Alliance) standardizes the interfaces inside the base station so operators can mix vendors. It splits the base station into three parts:

  • on the tower. Antennas, amplifiers, the lowest-level signal processing.
  • an ordinary server near the tower doing real-time baseband work: scheduling, error correction, beamforming math.
  • software in a data center or cloud handling the less time-critical protocol layers.

The key standard is the , which defines exactly which signal-processing steps happen in the radio and which happen in the server, connected by plain Ethernet (eCPRI). That standard is the only reason a chip company like Qualcomm can sell what is effectively a full base station design to a carrier like SpaceX without Ericsson in the room.

  • sells : chips and reference designs that radio makers (or ambitious customers) build into products. It is betting on , which runs the entire Layer 1 signal-processing pipeline on a dedicated DSP card (the X100) instead of bouncing data between a general-purpose CPU and an accelerator, the "lookaside" approach Intel long championed (it has since built the accelerator into its Xeon chips). Qualcomm's pitch is cheaper servers, lower power and fewer bottlenecks. The X100 card draws at most 35 W, according to Qualcomm's product brief, and at network scale every watt saved adds up.
  • is pushing on GPUs through its Aerial platform: a cell site that runs the radio and AI inference on the same hardware. Qualcomm's Malladi isn't convinced: "AI-based RAN is a lot more than just throw a GPU at it, and you're done."
  • supply competing baseband silicon, inline and lookaside respectively.
  • Startups and software players: (chiefly a cloud-native core and RAN software vendor, which quit making macro radios in 2025), , (the arm that sells the software behind Rakuten's own Open RAN network in Japan), (Fujitsu's network business, spun out in 2025), and (AI-native signal processing), among others.

Open RAN's track record is mixed. Rakuten in Japan and Dish in the U.S. (until EchoStar wound its network down) proved it , though neither proved it . Integrating parts from multiple vendors turned out to be expensive and messy, which is why the radios and baseband in AT&T's "Open RAN" come almost entirely from Ericsson. The first third-party radio, from 1FINITY, only made its first call in 2025. SpaceX is taking a third path: one silicon vendor, its own software, and an engineering culture that would rather build than integrate.

5. The Hard Part: Building a National Network From Scratch

Rockets are hard. Getting a conditional use permit from a county planning board in suburban New Jersey may be harder. Here's what's in the way.

Cost: $100 billion, give or take a moon mission

Estimates are all over the map. BNP Paribas analyst Sam McHugh reckons SpaceX would need to spend on a terrestrial network before it earns real revenue, . TD Cowen says more than $80 billion, and Bernstein $50–130 billion including spectrum. LightShed thinks the initial build could be as little as $10–15 billion. Verizon's Schulman, who is not a neutral party, says $300–500 billion. Some back-of-envelope numbers show why:

  • SpaceX doesn't own towers. It will lease space from American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA and others; the U.S. has roughly 450,000 cell sites of all kinds. Lease brokers put the ground rent that tower companies pay landowners at around , with urban rooftops at $4,000+. A carrier renting space a tower typically pays more than that, and leases usually rise about 3% a year. Even at a lowball $1,500/month, 50,000 sites comes to before buying a single radio.
  • Equipment and installation. Radios, antennas, servers, power systems, structural analysis, crane time and tower crews. This can run well into six figures for a new site, less for adding gear to an existing one.
  • Electricity at every site, plus a fiber or microwave link to carry its traffic back to the core.
  • Stores, marketing, handset subsidies and customer care. The incumbents spend billions a year on this alone, and most of it is money spent getting people to switch.

SpaceX has unusual advantages here: a Starlink broadband business that throws off cash, the ability to raise money at an enormous valuation, and a satellite layer that can cover rural areas, so it doesn't have to build towers everywhere the incumbents did.

But deep pockets have a lot of pockets. Since swallowing Elon Musk's xAI in February 2026, SpaceX has been pouring money into AI data centers: capital spending hit a reported $28.5 billion in the first half of 2026, more than triple a year earlier, with most of it going to AI infrastructure such as xAI's Colossus supercomputers in Memphis. Investors knocked the stock down about 13% when that number came out. Every dollar spent on GPUs is a dollar not spent on tower leases. If AI and 5G end up competing for the same budget, it's not obvious the cell towers win.

Spectrum: 80 MHz vs. 400 MHz

Here's the number from earlier. SpaceX's terrestrial holdings total roughly , and some of that is uplink-only. T-Mobile has nearly . Verizon and AT&T each have hundreds of MHz too, including wide TDD mid-band channels (C-band, 2.5 GHz, 3.45 GHz) that are ideal for massive MIMO.

Spectrum is capacity. With a fifth of the airwaves, SpaceX has to squeeze far more out of every MHz, which is why 64T64R FDD massive MIMO and Qualcomm's AI-driven beam prediction are central to the plan and not just marketing. Expect SpaceX to show up at every future FCC auction, starting with the upper C-band auction (160 MHz at 3.98–4.14 GHz), due by July 2027. (An AWS-3 re-auction already wrapped up in June 2026, raising about $3.5 billion.)

There's also a band-sharing puzzle: the same 2 GHz spectrum is supposed to serve both towers and satellites. Keeping the two from interfering, especially near the edges of tower coverage where a phone could hear both, takes careful coordination, and it's a novel problem.

Time: towers don't launch on Starship

Dish took about three years from the Sprint merger to cover roughly 70% of the U.S. population, and it struggled with indoor coverage and actual customer uptake the whole way. The physical rollout is limited by:

  • : thousands of local jurisdictions, each with its own process.
  • : the pool of certified climbers is finite, and the incumbents are already booking them.
  • : a 64T64R massive MIMO radio is heavy and catches a lot of wind. Many tower spots will need reinforcement.
  • : every site needs a fiber or microwave link, and a massive MIMO site moving gigabits needs fiber. Leasing or trenching it, site by site, is slow.

Phones: the quiet dependency

Your phone has to support SpaceX's frequencies. The good news is that much of SpaceX's 2 GHz spectrum lines up with 5G (which Dish got into recent phones, iPhones included) and band n66, and the 800 MHz block sits inside band 26, which nearly every U.S. phone supports. One snag: Apple's phones don't list the 4G LTE version of band 70. The less good news: carrier certification, eSIM provisioning, Wi-Fi calling, VoNR voice, emergency-911 location accuracy and roaming agreements are all tedious, unglamorous work, and any one of them can sink a launch. It helps that Qualcomm makes most of the modems in question.

AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile are not ignoring the sky. AT&T and Verizon have backed , a direct-to-phone satellite rival. T-Mobile is currently Starlink's own D2C partner, which makes the relationship awkward. In May 2026 the three carriers also agreed to pool spectrum in a joint satellite venture aimed at rural dead zones. SpaceX's CFO reportedly mused that they "wanted to create a cartel, maybe." And they all have one powerful tool: price cuts, funded by networks they paid off years ago.

As recently as September 2026, SpaceX's CFO was publicly hedging on whether it would build a terrestrial network at all, keeping options open for an MVNO arrangement or rooftop "femtocells" next to Starlink dishes. The Qualcomm deal suggests the company has made up its mind. Still, signing a supply contract is the easy part.

6. Milestones to Watch, 2026–2036

Near term (2026–2027): Paper and steel

  • FCC filings and master lease agreements. How many sites, which markets first, and with which tower companies. Watch for an American Tower or Crown Castle master lease announcement. It would be the first hard evidence of real scale.
  • Boost Mobile acquisition. If it closes, SpaceX gets millions of customers and a roaming bridge on day one.
  • Starlink Mobile V2 satellites on Starship (from mid-2027). These next-generation satellites carry the "full 5G" satellite layer. Each Starship launch matters.
  • EchoStar closing (around late 2027) and FCC approval of the Grain 800 MHz deal.
  • First cell sites go up (2027). Watch where the first clusters appear, and for any trial service. When drive-test data shows up on Ookla or Opensignal, the network is real.

Medium term (2028–2030): Show me the subscribers

  • The satellite 5G service is targeted for early 2028; watch for the terrestrial launch date. Pricing will tell you the strategy: aggressive undercutting or a premium "never offline" tier.
  • , especially iPhone. If Apple certifies a carrier, that carrier is real.
  • Population coverage claims vs. reality. Can SpaceX reach 50%+ of the population with good service? This is where Dish struggled.
  • Subscriber numbers and churn. In wireless, adding customers gets the headlines, but keeping them is what makes the money.
  • The upper C-band auction (2027), or more secondary-market deals.

Long term (2030–2036): The 6G turn

  • 6G standards (3GPP Release 21, ~2028–2029) and first 6G deployments (~2030). Satellite links are being designed into 6G from the start, which plays to SpaceX's strengths. Qualcomm is already floating a "giga-MIMO" concept with 128 or 256 transmitters and receivers per radio, and Malladi says the deal will "lay the foundation for AI-native 6G."
  • The end goal is a single core network, one phone number, and handoffs between tower and satellite that nobody notices. If SpaceX gets there first, the dead zone stops being a fact of life and becomes a product choice.
  • The market structure question. By the mid-2030s, either the U.S. has a durable fourth carrier with its own satellites, or there's one more company dividing up a former challenger's spectrum. There's not much middle ground.

SpaceX is doing something no operator has tried: building a cellular network from the sky down, with satellites for coverage, towers for capacity, and Qualcomm silicon to make the towers cheap and power-efficient enough to deploy by the tens of thousands.

The technology is plausible. The spectrum is thin but usable. The money exists, at least for SpaceX. What remains is the unglamorous work that has humbled every challenger before it: leases, permits, crews, phone certification, customer care and price wars.

SpaceX has a habit of turning "impossible" into "late, but done." Phone networks are a slower industry, measured in zoning variances instead of launch windows. Either way, the next few years will be interesting, and probably good news for anyone's phone bill.

Even if SpaceX stumbles, the industry is better off for the attempt. In 2023 I wrote an obituary, "R.I.P. 'Innovation in Mobile' (2015–2023)", blaming three killers: mergers that wiped out independent carriers, the big three swallowing the MVNOs, and spectrum priced beyond any challenger's reach. SpaceX is taking on all three. It has committed roughly $28 billion to spectrum, and, shut out as an MVNO, it is building its own network as an independent carrier. Even if it never wins, it forces everyone else to move. Maybe the obituary was premature.

In my 2020 parody, fake-Elon bragged about never paying for cell sites or backhaul. Real SpaceX is about to pay for both, which is the most grown-up thing a rocket company has ever done. Master plan amendment, Step 3b: If it works, your next dead zone might just be a fond memory.

The chroma-green satellites are still pending. Don't tell anyone.
